Elastic Response and Instabilities of Anomalous Hall Crystals

Félix Desrochers Email: felix.desrochers@mail.utoronto.ca Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 1A7, Canada    Mark R. Hirsbrunner Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 1A7, Canada    Joe Huxford Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 1A7, Canada    Adarsh S. Patri Affiliation:  Department of Physics and Astronomy & Stewart Blusson Quantum Matter Institute, University of British Columbia, Vancouver BC, Canada, V6T 1Z4    T. Senthil Affiliation:  Department of Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02139, USA    Yong Baek Kim Email: ybkim@physics.utoronto.ca Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario M5S 1A7, Canada
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Anomalous Hall crystals (AHCs) are exotic phases of matter that simultaneously break continuous translation symmetry and exhibit the quantum anomalous Hall effect. AHCs have recently been proposed to explain the observation of an integer quantum anomalous Hall phase in a multilayer graphene system. Despite intense theoretical and experimental interest, little is known about the mechanical properties of AHCs. We study the elastic properties of AHCs first by using a continuum model with quadratic dispersion and uniform Berry curvature. We find using time-dependent Hartree-Fock that the stiffness of the AHC is an order of magnitude smaller than that of the WC, which we attribute to the finite Chern number of the AHC preventing exponential localization of the charge density. By modifying the dispersion relation to include a local minimum modeled after that of rhombohedral pentalayer graphene (R5G), we find that deformations away from the triangular lattice minimize the AHC’s kinetic energy, which overwhelms the small stiffness and triggers a mechanical instability. Using a microscopic model of R5G, we observe a similar mechanical instability over an experimentally relevant parameter regime. We conclude that the topologically limited stiffness of AHCs makes them susceptible to mechanical instabilities, an important consideration when interpreting experiments in terms of AHCs.

Introduction.— It has long been known that strong interactions in electronic systems can spontaneously break continuous translation symmetry, leading to the formation of Wigner crystals  [64, 46, 4, 60]. In the presence of external magnetic fields, such systems can also exhibit the quantum Hall effect, forming what is called a Hall crystal [19, 29, 30, 59, 60]. Comparatively little is understood about related phases that exhibit the quantum Hall effect with no external field, spontaneously breaking both translation and time-reversal symmetry. These systems, dubbed anomalous Hall crystals (AHCs), have become a topic of intense theoretical study [15, 74, 13, 55, 14, 33, 68, 56, 57, 45, 71, 73, 70] in the wake of recent experimental results on moiré platforms [38, 39, 67, 62, 2, 8]. In particular, the excitement follows from reports of the integer and fractional quantum anomalous Hall (IQAH/FQAH) effects in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene (R5G) slightly misaligned with a hexagonal boron nitride substrate (i.e., a R5G/hBN moiré heterostructure) [38].

The IQAH is seen in these experiments when the first conduction band is filled (ν=1\nu=1 with respect to the moiré unit cell). The origin of this IQAH state is quite unconventional, as numerical studies show that the non-interacting band structure is metallic for experimentally relevant parameters. The isolated |𝒞|=1|\mathcal{C}|=1 Chern band only appears with the inclusion of the Coulomb interaction [20, 20, 33, 22, 23, 18, 15, 13, 14, 55, 74]. Experimentally, the IQAH and FQAH phases are observed when the system is subjected to a strong displacement field that polarizes the conduction electrons away from the moiré potential induced by the hBN substrate. The spatial separation between the hBN and the conduction electrons calls into question the role of the moiré potential in stabilizing the IQAH effect. Indeed, Hartree-Fock (HF) calculations support the presence of an AHC in the absence of a moiré potential, wherein strong interactions break translation symmetry to induce the formation of a Chern band [13, 74, 15, 14, 20, 33].

Despite the large body of recent work on AHCs, little is yet known about their mechanical properties. This is somewhat surprising, as it is clear even from earlier considerations that the elastic response of AHCs likely differs dramatically from that of conventional WCs [5, 10, 7, 17, 11]. A conventional WC is a triangular lattice of exponentially localized charges whose localization increases with the interaction strength. In contrast, the finite Chern number of AHCs presents a topological obstruction to forming exponentially localized orbitals [40, 6, 37], suggesting that real-space density modulations, and thus the mechanical stiffness, may be weaker in AHCs than WCs. A further consequence of this obstruction is that the semi-classical arguments for the stability of the triangular lattice in WCs cannot be applied to AHCs [5]. To the contrary, recent theoretical works on R5G hinted that the triangular lattice AHC phase may be unstable to unit cell doubling deformations, both via study of the collective modes obtained through time-dependent Hartree-Fock [33] and by direct comparison with calculations on enlarged unit cells [73]. However, a more comprehensive perspective beyond these specific instabilities is pressingly needed.

In this letter, we study the elastic response of AHCs to lattice deformations. We first study AHCs in a simple ideal parent band continuum model of interacting electrons with a quadratic dispersion and constant Berry curvature [56]. Using time-dependent Hartree-Fock (tdHF) numerics and analytical calculations based on a variational AHC ansatz [56], we conclude that the mechanical stiffness of the AHC is an order of magnitude weaker than the WC. This result indicates that small perturbations may drive the stiffness to a negative value, meaning that the AHC is susceptible to mechanical instabilities. To explore this possibility, we compute the stiffness of the parent band model with the quadratic dispersion replaced by one that emulates the low-energy dispersion of R5G. We show that the presence of a minimum in the dispersion near the Brillouin zone (BZ) boundary allows lattice deformations to reduce the kinetic energy. This change slightly reduces the stiffness of the WC, but makes the AHC mechanically unstable over a wide range of interaction strengths. We also apply a similar analysis to a realistic continuum model of R5G, finding again that the triangular lattice AHC is mechanically unstable over an experimentally relevant parameter regime. We conclude with a discussion of the implications of these results and important topics for future research.

They encode the quantum geometry of the band and are taken to be

ℱ⁡(𝒌,𝒒)=exp⁡[−ℬ4​(|𝒌−𝒒|2+2​i​𝒌×𝒒)],\displaystyle\mathcal{F}\left(\bm{k},\bm{q}\right)=\exp[-\frac{\mathcal{B}}{4}\left(\left|\bm{k}-\bm{q}\right|^{2}+2i\bm{k}\times\bm{q}\right)], (1)

where 𝒌×𝒒≡kx​qy−ky​qx\bm{k}\times\bm{q}\equiv k_{x}q_{y}-k_{y}q_{x} [56]. This choice of form factor corresponds to a band with uniform Berry curvature ℬ⁡(𝒌)=ℬ\mathcal{B}(\bm{k})=\mathcal{B} and a Fubini-Study metric gμ​νFS​(𝒌)=12​ℬ​δμ​νg_{\mu\nu}^{\mathrm{FS}}(\bm{k})=\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{B}\delta_{\mu\nu} that saturates the trace Tr⁡[gμ​νFS​(𝒌)]≥|ℬ⁡(𝒌)|\operatorname{Tr}\left[g_{\mu\nu}^{\mathrm{FS}}(\bm{k})\right]\geq|\mathcal{B}(\bm{k})| condition bound [43, 69]. We note that the parent band form factor (1) is the same as for the lowest Landau level (LLL) with magnetic length ℓB2=ℬ\ell_{B}^{2}=\mathcal{B}, making the parent band model a dispersive analog of the LLL with unrestricted momentum [56].

When ℬ=0\mathcal{B}=0, the parent band model describes the usual two-dimensional electron gas and exhibits a transition from a Fermi liquid to a WC for strong interactions. In contrast, if a sufficiently large Berry flux threads the first BZ formed by the resulting crystal, the Fermi liquid instead transitions to an AHC with Chern number given by the integer nearest to ℬ​A1BZ/2​π\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}/2\pi, where A1BZA_{\text{1BZ}} is the area of the first BZ. This nearest integer rounding of the Berry curvature can be understood in terms of a Berry-flux quantization condition [14] (see supplemental material 11 1 See Supplemental Material [INSERT URL] for details on the elastic modulus tensor, Hartree-Fock and time-dependent Hartree-Fock implementations, analytical AHC energy derivations in the strong interaction regime, and additional numerical results for rhombohedral pentalayer graphene, which includes Refs. [31, 47, 48, 51, 28, 32, 34, 52, 25, 65, 3, 44, 72, 26, 27].). The unit cell and first BZ area of the AHC are determined by the electronic density, such that there is one electron per unit cell (i.e., filling unity ν=1\nu=1).

This idealized model is a useful approximation for spin- and valley-polarized systems with a low electronic density, in which the atomic BZ is irrelevant, and the Berry curvature perceived by electrons near the band edge is approximately constant. Although highly simplified, it offers an analytically tractable model that can be compared with numerical calculations employing more realistic models. In what follows, we set m=1/2m=1/2 and the length of the reciprocal lattice vectors to unity (i.e., |𝑮1,△|=1|\bm{G}_{1,\triangle}|=1) such that energy is measured in units of |𝑮1,△|2/2​m|\bm{G}_{1,\triangle}|^{2}/2m.

We plot in Fig. 1 (a, b) the ground state charge density of the WC (ℬ​A1BZ=0)(\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=0) and AHC (ℬ​A1BZ=2​π)(\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=2\pi) phases of the parent band model obtained via self-consistent Hartree-Fock (see supplemental material [41]). The charge density variation of the WC is orders of magnitude larger than that of the AHCs, confirming that the topological obstruction to constructing maximally localized Wannier functions drastically reduces real-space density modulations of the AHCs. Furthermore, the overall spatial patterns obtained are dissimilar: the WC forms a triangular network of localized charges (Fig. 1(a)), whereas the AHCs form a honeycomb structure (Fig. 1(b)) [71, 13, 74]. In Fig. 1(c, d), we plot the charge density variation as a function of VcV_{c} for the WC (ℬ​A1BZ=0)(\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=0) and a range of AHC phases (ℬ​A1BZ=2​π, 4​π, 6​π)(\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=2\pi,\,4\pi,\,6\pi), showing that the charge becomes more localized in the WC as the interaction strength increases, but the opposite occurs in the AHCs. The low-charge-density modulation is further exacerbated for larger Chern numbers. These findings indicate that WCs and AHCs may have disparate mechanical properties. In the next section, we specifically study how the mechanical stiffness of each phase differs.

Parent band stiffness.—To compute the mechanical stiffness of WCs and AHCs in the parent band model, we assume the system crystallizes in a triangular lattice with basis vectors 𝑨1=2​π​(1,1/3)\bm{A}_{1}=2\pi(1,1/\sqrt{3}) and 𝑨2=2​π​(0,2/3)\bm{A}_{2}=2\pi(0,2/\sqrt{3}), such that the lattice site positions are 𝑹=m​𝑨1+n​𝑨2\bm{R}=m\bm{A}_{1}+n\bm{A}_{2} (m,n∈ℤm,n\in\mathbb{Z}). We apply deformations to the lattice of the form 𝑹′=𝑹+𝒖⁡(𝒓)=m​𝑨1′+n​𝑨2′\bm{R}^{\prime}=\bm{R}+\bm{u}(\bm{r})=m\bm{A}_{1}^{\prime}+n\bm{A}_{2}^{\prime}, where 𝑨1′\bm{A}_{1}^{\prime} and 𝑨2′\bm{A}_{2}^{\prime} are the basis vectors of the deformed lattice, and study how the ground state energy per electron varies as a function of the deformation. The second-order derivatives of the ground state energy per electron with respect to deformations can be directly related to the elastic coefficients that appear in the usual long-wavelength description of deformable media [11, 35]. The C6C_{6} point group symmetry of the triangular lattice restricts the elastic modulus matrix to have only two independent elements, C12C_{12} and C66C_{66}. We do not consider the area non-preserving deformations required to access C12C_{12}, and instead study the response to area-preserving dilations of the form 𝑨1′=(1+ud)​𝑨1\bm{A}_{1}^{\prime}=(1+u_{d})\bm{A}_{1} and 𝑨2′=(1+ud)−1​𝑨2\bm{A}_{2}^{\prime}=(1+u_{d})^{-1}\bm{A}_{2} (see Fig. 2(a)). From these deformations we obtain the C66C_{66} elastic coefficient as C66=3​n0/16​(∂2f/∂ud2)C_{66}=3n_{0}/16\left(\partial^{2}f/\partial u_{d}^{2}\right), where n0=N/An_{0}=N/A is the electron density and f=E0/Nf=E_{0}/N is the ground state energy per electron (see supplemental material [41]). Since we consider only a single elastic coefficient, we refer to C66C_{66} as the stiffness.

Figs. 2 (b) and (c) present the stiffness of topologically trivial (WC) and non-trivial (AHC) crystals arising in the parent band model at ℬ​A1BZ=0\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=0 and ℬ​A1BZ=2​π\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=2\pi, respectively. We compute the ground state energy via HF, incorporating the Madelung energy to alleviate finite-size effects arising from the long-range Coulomb interaction [24]. The momentum cutoff required for the energy to converge in this approach grows rapidly as VcV_{c} is increased, so we supplement this with a perturbative approach (dashed lines in Fig. 2 (c, e)) that is valid at large interaction strengths (see supplemental material [41]). We also obtain the correlation energy by further calculating the spectrum of excitations above the ground state via time-dependent Hartree-Fock (tdHF) (see supplemental material [41]). To clarify the role that the correlation energy plays, we separately compute the contributions to the stiffness coming from the HF and correlation energies, C66HFC_{66}^{\text{HF}} and C66corrC_{66}^{\text{corr}}, respectively, in addition to the total stiffness C66C_{66}.

First, analyzing the stiffness at the HF level, we see the stiffness of the WC, shown in Fig. 2(b), increases with VcV_{c}, as is classically expected [5, 11]. In contrast, the stiffness of the AHC with ℬ​A1BZ=2​π\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=2\pi is orders of magnitude weaker than for the WC, as demonstrated in panel (c) of Fig. 2. More strikingly, the stiffness of the AHCs unexpectedly decreases asymptotically to zero as the interaction strength increases.

This implies that the energy difference between different lattices also approaches zero, which we confirm by computing the HF ground state energy difference between the triangle and square lattices for AHCs in the End Matter. This is in stark contrast to the same energy comparison for the Wigner crystal, where the energy difference increases with the interaction strength (see End Matter). From an elastic point of view, the AHC thus becomes more “fluid-like” as interactions increase. We emphasize that even in this limit where all lattice shapes are degenerate, the system remains an electronic crystal with a finite charge gap, distinct from a Fermi liquid. We also point out that the stiffness is greater for larger Chern number AHCs because the band-projected interaction V~𝒌1​𝒌2​𝒌3​𝒌4\tilde{V}_{\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\bm{k}_{3}\bm{k}_{4}} is more strongly suppressed at larger Berry curvature as a result of the Gaussian prefactor in the form factors (1).

This decaying stiffness can be qualitatively understood by noting that the trace condition violation, bandwidth, and Berry curvature variation all decrease with stronger interactions in the AHC [56]. Indeed, the energetics of the parent band model is dominated by the Fock term, which is minimized when the trace condition violation of the filled HF band is reduced [56, 1]. Therefore, strong interactions drive the system to the ideal flatband limit [9, 61, 36, 16]. This, combined with the vanishing Berry curvature fluctuations, indicates that the emergent HF ground state closely resembles a filled Landau level, i.e., a quantum Hall fluid [43, 49, 42, 53]. However, going beyond mean-field, stronger interactions will couple the HF ground state to other states more strongly, and the true ground state will no longer be described by a filled Landau level Slater determinant.

Moving on to consider the contribution of the correlation energy to the stiffness, C66corr.,C_{66}^{\text{corr.}}, we again see the WC and AHC behave drastically differently. For the WC, plotted in Fig. 2 (b), C66corr.C_{66}^{\text{corr.}} is negative and decreases with increasing interaction strength. In contrast, C66corr.C_{66}^{\text{corr.}} for the AHC changes sign from negative to positive and appears to level off as VcV_{c} increases, shown in Fig. 2 (c). The reduction of the stiffness for the WC is expected, as HF famously underestimates the interaction strength at which the two-dimensional electron gas crystallizes, and the ground state at these intermediate interaction strengths should actually be a liquid [58, 50]. However, it appears that HF instead underestimates the stiffness of the AHC, which is stabilized by correlations to a finite value at large VcV_{c}.

Although the AHC does not flow to a state with vanishing stiffness at large interaction strengths when accounting for correlations, the total stiffness of the AHC is still an order of magnitude smaller than that of the WC. As such, we can conclude that the simple intuition provided in the introduction holds when considering quantum fluctuations: the topological obstruction limits the stiffness of AHCs. This limited stiffness may mean that small perturbations away from the ideal parent band model can drive a mechanical instability. We next study the stiffness of AHCs in the context of rhombohedral pentalayer graphene [13, 55, 15, 14, 74, 33].

Kinetic driven instability.—One of the ways that R5G differs from the ideal parent band model is in its dispersion, which possesses a distinct local minimum along a ring located at some finite momentum, as shown in Fig. 3 and the End Matter. We can study the effect of dispersion on stiffness in isolation by modifying the dispersion of the parent band while keeping the form factors unchanged. To do so, we replace the quadratic dispersion of the parent band model with ℰ⁡(𝒌)=D⁡((|𝒌|/k0)4−(|𝒌|/k0)2)\mathcal{E}(\bm{k})=D\left(\left(|\bm{k}|/k_{0}\right)^{4}-\left(|\bm{k}|/k_{0}\right)^{2}\right) which possesses a local minimum of depth DD at |𝒌|=k0|\bm{k}|=k_{0}. The band minimum in R5G occurs just outside the 1BZ for displacement fields that realize the IQAH, so we set k0=0.6​|𝑮|k_{0}=0.6|\bm{G}|. We show in the supplemental material that the kinetic energy can be reduced by deforming the lattice to access a larger portion of the dispersion minimum, which may drive an instability. Indeed, we see that the AHC is unstable over a large parameter range while the WC remains stable, as shown by the HF stiffness plotted in Fig. 3. This result indicates that minimizing the kinetic energy overwhelms the small stiffness of the AHC except for large values of Vc/DV_{c}/D, where the potential energy dominates the physics. We note that whenever the mechanical stiffness at the HF level is negative, the tdHF spectrum will be complex. Therefore, we cannot compute the stiffness arising from the correlation energy for this system. To confirm the pertinence of the above analysis, we present in the End Matter a numerical calculation of the AHC stiffness based on a microscopic model of R5G in an experimentally relevant parameter regime. Our analysis reveals a similar instability of the triangular lattice driven by kinetic energy.

Discussion.—We showed that AHCs in the ideal parent band model have a much weaker mechanical stiffness than conventional WCs, confirming the intuition that the topological obstruction of the Chern number limits the stiffness. The small stiffness indicates that mechanical instabilities of triangular lattice AHCs may arise beyond the ideal limit. Indeed, we confirm the presence of such an instability in a toy model with a Mexican hat dispersion and in a realistic microscopic model of rhombohedral multilayer graphene with a strong displacement field. Despite the specificity of the models we studied, our results are quite general, relying only on the finite Chern number of the AHC. The weak mechanical stiffness of AHCs also indirectly implies a low speed of sound and an overall low-energy phonon spectrum. These low-energy collective modes may have a sizeable entropic contribution at finite temperatures that could be important for understanding the thermal crossover (or transition) from the IQAH to the FQAH in R5G/hBN [39, 66, 21, 12, 54, 63, 45].

Several other important questions remain to be addressed in future studies. The recent observation of the IQAH over an extended range of filling and displacement fields in R5G/hBN [39] further motivates the study of density-varying deformations beyond the area-preserving transformations we focused on. Studying the response of AHCs to such deformations, either in the ideal limit or with more realistic models, would clarify the competition between the elastic and commensuration energies in the presence of a periodic potential, which is crucial for interpreting the experiment [45]. We also note that it may be possible to tune the stability of the putative AHC in R5G by varying the displacement field, given its kinetic origin and the displacement-field dependence of R5G’s dispersion. Furthermore, investigating such distortions should help evaluate the possibility of stabilizing fractional anomalous Hall crystals, as recently proposed in the parent-band model [57].

End Matter

Energy difference between lattices.—We have mentioned in the main text that the energy difference between AHCs with different lattices decreases with interaction strength for the ideal parent band. To show this convincingly, we present in Fig. 4(b) the HF ground state energy difference between the triangle and square lattices for AHCs with ℬ​A1BZ=2​π\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=2\pi, 4​π4\pi, and 6​π6\pi. We see that the energy difference decreases monotonically with interactions for 𝒞=1\mathcal{C}=1, 22, and 33. We note that the square lattice even appears lower in energy than the triangular lattice (Fig. 2(e)) at large interaction strengths, but this is an artifact arising from the finite momentum cutoff. Indeed, the perturbative calculation predicts that the triangular lattice always remains stable and lower in energy than the square lattice for large VcV_{c}. Computing the stiffness of the square lattice also shows that it is unstable to shear deformations towards the triangular lattice, for both the WC and AHC. This behavior of the energy difference for AHC is in stark contrast with the same comparison for the Wigner crystal (Fig. 4(a)). In this case, the energy difference grows with interaction strength.

Rhombohedral pentalayer graphene.—To further study possible instabilities of AHCs, we compute the HF stiffness of the AHC arising in R5G using an explicit microscopic model (see supplemental material [41] for details). We model the displacement field as a layer potential UdU_{d} and use a dual-gated screened interaction Vcsc​(𝒒)=e2​tanh⁡(|𝒒|​ds)/(2​ϵ0​ϵ​|𝒒|)V_{c}^{\mathrm{sc}}(\bm{q})=e^{2}\tanh\left(|\bm{q}|d_{s}\right)/(2\epsilon_{0}\epsilon|\bm{q}|), where ϵ\epsilon is the dielectric constant and dsd_{s} the distance separating the metallic gates. We focus on the experimentally relevant parameter regime, i.e., a strong displacement field Ud=−36U_{d}=-36 meV, electronic density consistent with a filled moiré conduction band (ν=1\nu=1), and a twist angle of θ=0.77∘\theta=0.77^{\circ}. Our HF calculations assume spin-valley polarization, retain only the lowest nbandsn_{\text{bands}} conduction bands, and use the triangular lattice with an orientation that minimizes the ground state energy as the starting point. This orientation is found to respect the C3C_{3} symmetry of the underlying microscopic model (see supplemental material [41] for details).

Fig. 5(b) shows the evolution of C66HFC_{66}^{\text{HF}} with the interaction strength (controlled by the inverse dielectric constant 1/ϵ1/\epsilon). The stiffness is negative for the entire range of ϵ\epsilon considered, signaling the mechanical instability of the triangular lattice. To verify that this instability is not due to finite-size effects, we compare the ground state energy of the triangular lattice (ud=0u_{d}=0) and a C3C_{3}-symmetry breaking dilated triangular lattice (ud=−0.15u_{d}=-0.15) for a range of system sizes (Fig. 5(c)) and number of conduction bands (Fig. 5(d)). The ground state energy of the distorted lattice is always smaller, even when extrapolated to the limit of infinite system size or number of bands. This confirms the mechanical instability of the previously assumed triangular lattice AHC in R5G for an experimentally relevant parameter regime within the HF approximation. In the supplemental material, we consider how the kinetic, Hartree, and Fock energies change as functions of udu_{d}, and further show that lowering the displacement field such that the local minimum of the dispersion disappears stabilizes the triangular lattice AHC. We note that even when including a moiré potential induced by a hexagonal boron nitride substrate on the bottom layer (with a twist angle of θ=0.77∘\theta=0.77^{\circ}) and assuming a weakly pinned triangular AHC aligned with the moiré lattice, the deformed lattice configuration remains energetically favorable (Fig. 5(c)). Taken together, these results confirm that the instability is driven by the kinetic energy, as predicted by our analysis of the modified parent band model.

I Mechanical response

In this section, we comment on how the shear and dilation stiffnesses defined in the main text are related to the usual elastic coefficients that appear in the long wavelength description of a deformable medium. The deformation energy in the continuum limit can be written as

Δ​E=12​Ca​b​c​d​εa​b​εc​d,\displaystyle\Delta E=\frac{1}{2}C_{abcd}\varepsilon_{ab}\varepsilon_{cd}, (S1)

where the symmetric strain tensor is defined as

εa​b​(𝒓)\displaystyle\varepsilon_{ab}(\bm{r}) =12​(∂ua​(𝒓)∂rb+∂ub​(𝒓)∂ra)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\partialderivative{u_a(\boldsymbol{r})}{r_b}+\partialderivative{u_{b}(\boldsymbol{r})}{r_{a}}\right) (S2)

with the displacement vector 𝒖⁡(𝒓)\bm{u}(\bm{r}) and a,b∈{x,y}a,b\in\{x,y\}. The elastic modulus tensor (or stiffness tensor) Ca​b​c​dC_{abcd} must satisfy the generic symmetry constraints Ca​b​c​d=Cb​a​c​d=Ca​b​d​c=Cc​d​a​bC_{abcd}=C_{bacd}=C_{abdc}=C_{cdab}, such that there are only six independent components (Cx​x​x​x,Cy​y​y​y,Cx​y​x​y,Cx​x​y​y,Cx​x​x​y,Cy​y​x​yC_{xxxx},C_{yyyy},C_{xyxy},C_{xxyy},C_{xxxy},C_{yyxy}) in two-dimensions. Using Voigt notation, the deformation energy can then be written concisely as [35]

Δ​E\displaystyle\Delta E =12​∫d2​r​(εx​x,εy​y,2​εx​y)​(C11C12C16C12C22C26C16C26C66)​(εx​xεy​y2​εx​y),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int d^{2}r\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix\varepsilon_{xx}, \varepsilon_{yy}, 2\varepsilon_{xy}\endlx@physics@matrix)\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix C_{11} & C_{12} & C_{16} \\ C_{12} & C_{22} & C_{26} \\ C_{16} & C_{26} & C_{66}\endlx@physics@matrix)\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix\varepsilon_{xx} \\ \varepsilon_{yy} \\ 2\varepsilon_{xy}\endlx@physics@matrix), (S3)

where C11=Cx​x​x​xC_{11}=C_{xxxx}, C22=Cy​y​y​yC_{22}=C_{yyyy}, C12=Cx​x​y​yC_{12}=C_{xxyy}, C16=Cx​x​x​yC_{16}=C_{xxxy}, C26=Cy​y​x​yC_{26}=C_{yyxy}, and C66=Cx​y​x​yC_{66}=C_{xyxy}. The C6C_{6} point group symmetry imposes that [35, 11]

C26\displaystyle C_{26} =C16=0\displaystyle=C_{16}=0 (S4a)
C11\displaystyle C_{11} =C22=2​C66+C12.\displaystyle=C_{22}=2C_{66}+C_{12}. (S4b)

The elastic energy can then be written using only two stiffness coefficients

Δ​E\displaystyle\Delta E =12​∫d2​r​(εx​x,εy​y,2​εx​y)​(2​C66+C12C120C122​C66+C12000C66)​(εx​xεy​y2​εx​y).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int d^{2}r\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix\varepsilon_{xx}, \varepsilon_{yy}, 2 \varepsilon_{xy}\endlx@physics@matrix)\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix 2C_{66} + C_{12} & C_{12} & 0\\ C_{12} & 2C_{66} + C_{12} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & C_{66}\endlx@physics@matrix)\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix\varepsilon_{xx} \\ \varepsilon_{yy} \\ 2 \varepsilon_{xy}\endlx@physics@matrix). (S5)

We also note that the lattice structure is stable if the elastic modulus matrix is positive definite. That is, the triangular lattice is stable if

C66>0\displaystyle C_{66}>0 (S6a)
and
C12+C66\displaystyle C_{12}+C_{66} >0.\displaystyle>0. (S6b)

The coefficients can be extracted by computing the ground state energy as a function of the deformation strength for specific distortions. Below, we derive the explicit relation between the elastic coefficients and the curvature of the deformation energy for shear and area-preserving dilations.

We first discuss how to parameterize lattice deformations. The basis vectors for a generic two-dimensional lattice can be written as

𝑨1\displaystyle\bm{A}_{1} =a0​η​(sin⁡(φ),cos⁡(φ))\displaystyle=a_{0}\eta\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix\sin(\varphi), \cos(\varphi)\endlx@physics@matrix) (S7a)
𝑨2\displaystyle\bm{A}_{2} =a0​(0,1).\displaystyle=a_{0}\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix 0,1\endlx@physics@matrix). (S7b)

For the triangular lattice, we have η=1\eta=1 and φ=π/3\varphi=\pi/3. The associated basis vectors of the reciprocal lattice are

𝑮1\displaystyle\bm{G}_{1} =2​πa0​η​(csc⁡(φ),0)\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{a_{0}\eta}\left(\csc(\varphi),0\right) (S8a)
𝑮2\displaystyle\bm{G}_{2} =2​πa0​(−cot⁡(φ),1).\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{a_{0}}\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix-\cot(\varphi), 1\endlx@physics@matrix). (S8b)

Suppose the initial lattice sites 𝑹=m​𝑨1+n​𝑨2\bm{R}=m\bm{A}_{1}+n\bm{A}_{2} (m,n∈ℤm,n\in\mathbb{Z}) are displaced by 𝒖⁡(𝒓)\bm{u}(\bm{r}). The new sites of the deformed lattice are 𝑹′=m​𝑨1+n​𝑨2+𝒖⁡(𝒓)\bm{R}^{\prime}=m\bm{A}_{1}+n\bm{A}_{2}+\bm{u}(\bm{r}), which can also be expressed as 𝑹′=m​𝑨1′+n​𝑨2′\bm{R}^{\prime}=m\bm{A}_{1}^{\prime}+n\bm{A}_{2}^{\prime}, where we have introduced the basis vectors for the deformed lattice

𝑨1′\displaystyle\bm{A}_{1}^{\prime} =a0′​η′​(sin⁡(φ′),cos⁡(φ′))\displaystyle=a_{0}^{\prime}\eta^{\prime}\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix\sin(\varphi'), \cos(\varphi')\endlx@physics@matrix) (S9a)
𝑨2′\displaystyle\bm{A}_{2}^{\prime} =a0′​(0,1).\displaystyle=a_{0}^{\prime}\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix 0,1\endlx@physics@matrix). (S9b)

The corresponding reciprocal lattice vectors of the deformed lattice are

𝑮1′\displaystyle\bm{G}_{1}^{\prime} =2​πa0′​η′​(csc⁡(φ′),0)\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{a_{0}^{\prime}\eta^{\prime}}\left(\csc(\varphi'),0\right) (S10a)
𝑮2′\displaystyle\bm{G}_{2}^{\prime} =2​πa0′​(−cot⁡(φ′),1).\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{a_{0}^{\prime}}\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix-\cot(\varphi'), 1\endlx@physics@matrix). (S10b)

A deformation can thus be parameterized by the evolution of a0′a_{0}^{\prime}, η′\eta^{\prime}, and φ′\varphi^{\prime} as a function of the deformation strength u0u_{0}. For instance, a shear deformation of the form ux​(𝒓)=0u_{x}(\bm{r})=0 and uy​(𝒓)=us​xu_{y}(\bm{r})=u_{s}x (for a lattice site 𝑹\bm{R}, xx is defined as x^⋅𝐑\hat{x}\cdot\mathbf{R}) leads to

a0′\displaystyle a_{0}^{\prime} =a0\displaystyle=a_{0} (S11a)
η′\displaystyle\eta^{\prime} =η​1+2​us​sin⁡(φ)​cos⁡(φ)+us2​sin2⁡(φ)\displaystyle=\eta\sqrt{1+2u_{s}\sin(\varphi)\cos(\varphi)+u_{s}^{2}\sin^{2}(\varphi)} (S11b)
sin⁡(φ′)\displaystyle\sin\left(\varphi^{\prime}\right) =sin⁡(φ)1+2​us​sin⁡(φ)​cos⁡(φ)+us2​sin2⁡(φ).\displaystyle=\frac{\sin(\varphi)}{\sqrt{1+2u_{s}\sin(\varphi)\cos(\varphi)+u_{s}^{2}\sin^{2}(\varphi)}}. (S11c)

Using the above parameterization, the symmetric strain tensor components are εx​x=εy​y=0\varepsilon_{xx}=\varepsilon_{yy}=0 and εx​y=us/2\varepsilon_{xy}=u_{s}/2. Making this replacement in Eq. (S5), the deformation energy for a shear deformation is Δ​Eshear=A​us2​C66/2\Delta E_{\text{shear}}=Au_{s}^{2}C_{66}/2. Defining the deformation energy per electron as f=Δ​E/Nf=\Delta E/N, we then see that the shear stiffness defined in the main text is related to C66C_{66} by

∂2fshear∂us2|us→0=n0−1​C66,\displaystyle\left.\partialderivative[2]{f_{\text{shear}}}{u_s}\right|_{u_{s}\to 0}=n_{0}^{-1}C_{66}, (S12)

where the electronic density is n0=N/An_{0}=N/A.

In addition to shear deformations, we also study area-preserving dilations of the form

𝑨1′\displaystyle\bm{A}_{1}^{\prime} =(1+ud)​𝑨1\displaystyle=(1+u_{d})\bm{A}_{1} (S13)
𝑨2′\displaystyle\bm{A}_{2}^{\prime} =(1+ud)−1​𝑨2,\displaystyle=(1+u_{d})^{-1}\bm{A}_{2},

that can be parameterized by

a0′\displaystyle a_{0}^{\prime} =a0/(1+ud)\displaystyle=a_{0}/(1+u_{d}) (S14a)
η′\displaystyle\eta^{\prime} =(1+ud)2​η\displaystyle=(1+u_{d})^{2}\eta (S14b)
sin⁡(φ′)\displaystyle\sin\left(\varphi^{\prime}\right) =sin⁡(φ).\displaystyle=\sin(\varphi). (S14c)

The displacement vector then takes the form

ux​(𝒓)=ud​x,uy​(𝒓)=ud​(2+ud)​cot⁡(φ)1+ud​x−ud1+ud​y,\displaystyle u_{x}(\bm{r})=u_{d}x,\quad u_{y}(\bm{r})=\frac{u_{d}(2+u_{d})\cot{\varphi}}{1+u_{d}}x-\frac{u_{d}}{1+u_{d}}y, (S15)

such that the symmetric strain tensor components are

εx​x\displaystyle\varepsilon_{xx} =ud\displaystyle=u_{d} (S16a)
εy​y\displaystyle\varepsilon_{yy} =−ud1+ud\displaystyle=-\frac{u_{d}}{1+u_{d}} (S16b)
εx​y\displaystyle\varepsilon_{xy} =ud​(2+ud)2​(1+ud)​cot⁡(φ).\displaystyle=\frac{u_{d}(2+u_{d})}{2(1+u_{d})}\cot(\varphi). (S16c)

The corresponding deformation energy is

Δ​Edilation\displaystyle\Delta E_{\text{dilation}} =A​ud22​(1+ud)2​((C12+C66)​ud2+C66​(2+ud)2​csc2⁡(φ)),\displaystyle=A\frac{u_{d}^{2}}{2(1+u_{d})^{2}}\left((C_{12}+C_{66})u_{d}^{2}+C_{66}(2+u_{d})^{2}\csc^{2}(\varphi)\right), (S17)

which yields

∂2fdilation∂ud2|ud→0=4​n0−1​csc2⁡(φ)​C66=163​n0​C66.\displaystyle\left.\partialderivative[2]{f_{\text{dilation}}}{u_d}\right|_{u_{d}\to 0}=4n_{0}^{-1}\csc^{2}(\varphi)C_{66}=\frac{16}{3n_{0}}C_{66}. (S18)

Consequently, the curvature of the deformation energy for area-preserving dilations is also determined by C66C_{66} for the triangular lattice.

II Hartree-Fock calculations of the parent band model

II.1 Hartree-Fock decoupling

The Hartree-Fock approximation is a variational approach over the space of Slater determinant states. It amounts to a mean-field treatment of the quartic interaction term that leads to the Hartree and Fock terms

ℋH\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{H}} =1A​∑𝒌1​𝒌2𝒈1​𝒈2​𝒈3​𝒈4V⁡(𝒈1−𝒈4)​ℱ​(𝒌1+𝒈1,𝒌1+𝒈4)​ℱ​(𝒌2+𝒈2,𝒌2+𝒈3)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\\ \bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}\bm{g}_{3}\bm{g}_{4}\end{subarray}}V\left(\bm{g}_{1}-\bm{g}_{4}\right)\mathcal{F}\left(\bm{k}_{1}+\bm{g}_{1},\bm{k}_{1}+\bm{g}_{4}\right)\mathcal{F}\left(\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{g}_{2},\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{g}_{3}\right)
×δ⁡(𝒈1+𝒈2−𝒈3−𝒈4)​𝒫𝒈1​𝒈4​(𝒌1)​c𝒌2​𝒈2†​c𝒌2​𝒈3\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt\times\delta(\bm{g}_{1}+\bm{g}_{2}-\bm{g}_{3}-\bm{g}_{4})\mathcal{P}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{4}}(\bm{k}_{1})c_{\bm{k}_{2}\bm{g}_{2}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}_{2}\bm{g}_{3}} (S19a)
ℋF\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{F}} =−1A∑𝒌1​𝒌2𝒈1​𝒈2​𝒈3​𝒈4V(𝒌1+𝒈1−𝒌2−𝒈4)ℱ(𝒌1+𝒈1,𝒌2+𝒈4)ℱ(𝒌2+𝒈2,𝒌1+𝒈3)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{k}_{1}\bm{k}_{2}\\ \bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}\bm{g}_{3}\bm{g}_{4}\end{subarray}}V\left(\bm{k}_{1}+\bm{g}_{1}-\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{g}_{4}\right)\mathcal{F}\left(\bm{k}_{1}+\bm{g}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{g}_{4}\right)\mathcal{F}\left(\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{g}_{2},\bm{k}_{1}+\bm{g}_{3}\right)
×δ⁡(𝒈1+𝒈2−𝒈3−𝒈4)​𝒫𝒈1​𝒈3​(𝒌1)​c𝒌2​𝒈2†​c𝒌2​𝒈4,\displaystyle\hskip 85.35826pt\times\delta(\bm{g}_{1}+\bm{g}_{2}-\bm{g}_{3}-\bm{g}_{4})\mathcal{P}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{3}}(\bm{k}_{1})c_{\bm{k}_{2}\bm{g}_{2}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}_{2}\bm{g}_{4}}, (S19b)

where the density matrix

𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2​(𝒌)=⟨c𝒌​𝒈1†​c𝒌​𝒈2⟩\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}\left(\bm{k}\right)=\left\langle c_{\bm{k}\bm{g}_{1}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}\bm{g}_{2}}\right\rangle (S20)

is in a one-to-one correspondence with Slater determinant states.

Following the approach used in Refs. [56, 57], we remove the long-ranged part of the Coulomb interaction by excluding V⁡(𝒒=0)V(\bm{q}=0) from the momentum sum (and do the same for the sum over 𝒈\bm{g} in the Hartree term). The 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 gives a contribution V⁡(0)​(N2−N)/2​AV(0)(N^{2}-N)/2A, which is irrelevant in our study since we always keep the electronic density constant. We follow this prescription throughout our analysis using Hartree-Fock and the variational ansatz.

II.2 Details about the Hartree-Fock numerics

To find the optimal density matrix, one has to solve for 𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2​(𝒌)\mathcal{P}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}\left(\bm{k}\right) self-consistently. In our case, we numerically solve the self-consistency equation (S20). To do so, the first Brillouin zone is discretized as

𝒌=in1​𝑮1+jn2​𝑮2\displaystyle\bm{k}=\frac{i}{n_{1}}\bm{G}_{1}+\frac{j}{n_{2}}\bm{G}_{2} (S21)

where i∈{0,1,2,…​n1−1}i\in\{0,1,2,\ldots n_{1}-1\}, and j∈{0,1,2,…​n2−1}j\in\{0,1,2,\ldots n_{2}-1\}. The kinetic, Hartree, and Fock terms are constructed by including all reciprocal lattice points 𝒈=a​𝑮1+b​𝑮2\bm{g}=a\bm{G}_{1}+b\bm{G}_{2} (a,b∈ℤa,b\in\mathbb{Z}) within a cutoff |𝒈|≤Λ​|𝑮1||\bm{g}|\leq\Lambda|\bm{G}_{1}|. Our simulations include the nΓ=97n_{\Gamma}=97 closest reciprocal lattice points (Λ≈5\Lambda\approx 5). With these values, we find good convergence of the self-consistency conditions and ground state energy (see Sec. II.3). As illustrated in Fig. S1(a), the density matrix occupation for the furthermost reciprocal lattice points with such cutoffs in the crystalline phases is usually less than 10−3010^{-30} for Vc/Au.c.=2V_{c}/A_{\text{u.c.}}=2. It decays more slowly when interactions increase (Fig. S1(b)).

To solve the self-consistency conditions, we randomly initialize a density matrix 𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2(0)​(𝒌)\mathcal{P}^{(0)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}\left(\bm{k}\right) and update it using periodic Pulay mixing, a method also known as periodic direct inversion of the iterative subspace (DIIS) [47, 48, 31, 51]. At every iteration, the residual ρ𝒈1​𝒈2(n)​(𝒌)\rho^{(n)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k}) is evaluated

ρ𝒈1​𝒈2(n)​(𝒌)\displaystyle\rho^{(n)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k}) =⟨c𝒌​𝒈1†​c𝒌​𝒈2⟩(n)−𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2(n)​(𝒌),\displaystyle=\left\langle c_{\bm{k}\bm{g}_{1}}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}\bm{g}_{2}}\right\rangle^{(n)}-\mathcal{P}^{(n)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k}), (S22)

where ⟨A⟩(n)\left\langle A\right\rangle^{(n)} denotes an average computed from the ground state of the Hartree-Fock Hamiltonian (S19) with density matrix 𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2(n)​(𝒌)\mathcal{P}^{(n)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k}). The density matrix used for the next iteration is then computed using simple mixing

𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2(n+1)​(𝒌)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}^{(n+1)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k}) =𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2(n)​(𝒌)+αmixing​ρ𝒈1​𝒈2(n)​(𝒌),\displaystyle=\mathcal{P}^{(n)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k})+\alpha_{\text{mixing}}\rho^{(n)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k}), (S23)

where αmixing∈(0,1]\alpha_{\text{mixing}}\in(0,1]. However, after every kdiisk_{\text{diis}} steps, the new density matrix is instead evaluated using DIIS. It is given by a linear combination of the ndiisn_{\text{diis}} previous steps

𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2(n+1)​(𝒌)=cn​𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2(n)​(𝒌)+cn−1​𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2(n−1)​(𝒌)+…+cn−ndiis​𝒫𝒈1​𝒈2(n−ndiis)​(𝒌)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}^{(n+1)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k})=c_{n}\mathcal{P}^{(n)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k})+c_{n-1}\mathcal{P}^{(n-1)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k})+\ldots+c_{n-n_{\text{diis}}}\mathcal{P}^{(n-n_{\text{diis}})}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k}) (S24)

that minimizes the Euclidian norm of ∑i=0ndiiscn−i​ρ𝒈1​𝒈2(n−i)​(𝒌)\sum_{i=0}^{n_{\text{diis}}}c_{n-i}\rho^{(n-i)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k}) subject to the normalization constraint ∑i=0ndiiscn−i=1\sum_{i=0}^{n_{\text{diis}}}c_{n-i}=1. This is achieved by solving the linear system of equations

(Bn,nBn,n−1…Bn,n−ndiis−1Bn−1,nBn−1,n−1…Bn−1,n−ndiis−1⋱Bn−ndiis,nBn−ndiis,n−1…Bn−ndiis,n−ndiis−1111…0)​(cncn−1cn−2cn−ndiisλ)=(00001),\displaystyle\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix B_{n,n} & B_{n,n-1} & \ldots& B_{n, n-n_{\text{diis}}} & -1 \\ B_{n-1,n} & B_{n-1,n-1} & \ldots& B_{n-1, n-n_{\text{diis}}} & -1 \\ \vdots& \vdots& \ddots& \vdots& \vdots\\ B_{n-n_{\text{diis}},n} & B_{n-n_{\text{diis}},n-1} & \ldots& B_{n-n_{\text{diis}},n-n_{\text{diis}}} & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & \ldots& 0 \endlx@physics@matrix)\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix c_{n} \\ c_{n-1} \\c_{n-2} \\\vdots\\c_{n-n_{\text{diis}}} \\\lambda\endlx@physics@matrix)=\matrixquantity(\lx@physics@matrix 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots\\ 0 \\ 1 \endlx@physics@matrix), (S25)

where

Bi,j=∑𝒌​𝒈1​𝒈2(ρ𝒈1​𝒈2(i)​(𝒌))∗​ρ𝒈2​𝒈1(j)​(𝒌).\displaystyle B_{i,j}=\sum_{\bm{k}\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\rho^{(i)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k}))^{*}\rho^{(j)}_{\bm{g}_{2}\bm{g}_{1}}(\bm{k}). (S26)

The iteration is stopped when the infinity (or maximum) norm of the residual array is smaller than a threshold λthresh\lambda_{\text{thresh}}

‖ρ𝒈1​𝒈2(n)​(𝒌)‖∞=max⁡(|ρ𝒈1​𝒈2(n)​(𝒌)|)≤λthresh.\displaystyle\norm{\rho^{(n)}_{\boldsymbol{g}_1\boldsymbol{g}_2}(\boldsymbol{k})}_{\infty}=\max(|\rho^{(n)}_{\bm{g}_{1}\bm{g}_{2}}(\bm{k})|)\leq\lambda_{\text{thresh}}. (S27)

In this work, we use αmixing=0.9\alpha_{\text{mixing}}=0.9, kdiis=10k_{\text{diis}}=10, ndiis=5n_{\text{diis}}=5 and a threshold of λthresh=10−14\lambda_{\text{thresh}}=10^{-14}. A typical evolution of the residual norm and ground state energy when solving the self-consistency conditions is shown in Fig. S2.

II.3 Convergence

Our numerical approach is limited in accuracy by the finite momentum cutoff Λ\Lambda, or equivalently, the finite number of reciprocal lattice points nΓn_{\Gamma} included. Fig. S3 shows the evolution of the ground state energy per particle as nΓn_{\Gamma} increased for the triangular and square lattice in the AHC phase with ℬ​A1BZ=2​π\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=2\pi. We see that the ground state energy converges quickly with nΓn_{\Gamma}. More precisely, as is clear from the panels (b.1)-(b.2) that are displayed on a logarithmic scale, the ground state energy per particle decays exponentially with nΓn_{\Gamma} as

Eg.s.​(nΓ)\displaystyle E_{\text{g.s.}}(n_{\Gamma}) =Eg.s.​(nΓ→∞)−C​e−D​nΓ.\displaystyle=E_{\text{g.s.}}(n_{\Gamma}\to\infty)-Ce^{-Dn_{\Gamma}}. (S28)

From the figure, it can be observed that one needs to include more reciprocal lattice points to achieve a similar convergence of the ground state energy at larger interaction strengths. This is simply because the density matrix decays more slowly in momentum space for larger VcV_{c} (see Fig. S1). For nΓ=97n_{\Gamma}=97 (which is the number of reciprocal lattice points included for both the triangle and square lattice in the main text), the energy difference with the infinite cutoff extrapolated energy (i.e., Eg.s.​(nΓ→∞)E_{\text{g.s.}}(n_{\Gamma}\to\infty)) is on the order of 10−1410^{-14} for Vc/Au.c.=2V_{c}/A_{\text{u.c.}}=2 and 10−910^{-9} for Vc/Au.c.=8V_{c}/A_{\text{u.c.}}=8. Those energy differences are significantly smaller than those involved in the comparison between the triangular and square lattice ground state energies presented in the main text. The cutoffs used should thus be sufficiently large so as not to affect the reliability of our conclusions.

Next, calculations of the ground state energy also suffer from finite-size effects arising from the finite linear system size n1n_{1}. This typically leads to the ground state energy converging slowly as 1/n11/n_{1}, due to the long-range Coulomb interaction. To alleviate these effects, we incorporate the Madelung energy [24]. Incorporating the Madelung contribution yields excellent convergence even for small system size, as seen in Fig. S4.

II.4 Hartree-Fock Phase diagram

As supplemental results, we present in Fig. S5 a large HF phase diagram obtained by keeping the nΓ=61n_{\Gamma}=61 closest reciprocal lattice points and a finite system size of 21×2121\times 21. This phase diagram shows the transition from the Fermi liquid (FL) to the WC/AHC as the interaction is increased. It also shows the transition from the WC to the AHC with 𝒞=1\mathcal{C}=1 and between AHC with different Chern numbers. Those transitions happen when the closest integer to ℬ​A1BZ/(2​π)\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}/(2\pi) changes. This ‘rounding’ of the Berry curvature to the nearest integer was previously addressed in Ref. [14], where the Fock energy term is recast into a momentum space analog of a narrow superconducting ring in a background magnetic field, with the crystal order parameter and Berry curvature of the parent band taking the role of the superconducting order parameter and magnetic field, respectively. The subsequent ‘rounding’ of the Berry curvature is understood as the momentum-space analog of the flux-quantization condition.

III Time-dependent Hartree-Fock

Time-dependent Hartree-Fock (tdHF) is a method for studying neutral particle-hole excitations above the Hartree-Fock ground state [52, 28, 32, 34]. The creation operators for such excitations are defined as

Qν​𝒒†=∑φ,𝒌(Xφν​𝒒​(𝒌)​bφ,𝒒†​(𝒌)−Yφν​𝒒​(𝒌)​bφ,−𝒒​(𝒌)),Q^{\dagger}_{\nu\bm{q}}=\sum_{\varphi,\bm{k}}\left(X^{\nu\bm{q}}_{\varphi}(\bm{k})b^{\dagger}_{\varphi,\bm{q}}(\bm{k})-Y^{\nu\bm{q}}_{\varphi}(\bm{k})b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\varphi,-\bm{q}}(\bm{k})\right), (S29)

where φ\varphi labels pairs of particle and hole bands (ϕp,ϕh)(\phi_{p},\phi_{h}), bφ,𝒒†​(𝒌)=ηϕp†​(𝒌+𝒒)​ηϕh​(𝒌)b^{\dagger}_{\varphi,\bm{q}}(\bm{k})=\eta^{\dagger}_{\phi_{p}}(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\eta_{\phi_{h}}(\bm{k}) is a creation operator for an elementary particle-hole pair with momentum 𝒒\bm{q} and ηϕ†​(𝒌)\eta^{\dagger}_{\phi}(\bm{k}) is the creation operator for a HF eigenstate. Here, our notation allows multiple occupied (hole) bands, but in practice, we consider only a single occupied band. Below, we describe how to construct the tdHF equations from which the energies of these modes can be obtained, and show how to compute the correlation energy contributed by these modes.

The correlated ground state is defined as that which is annihilated by all Qν​𝒒Q_{\nu\bm{q}},

Qν​𝒒​|0⟩=0.Q_{\nu\bm{q}}\ket{0}=0. (S30)

As eigenstates of the Hamiltonian, these operators obey the Schrödinger equation,

[H,Qν​𝒒†]=ℏ​ων​𝒒​Qν​𝒒†,\left[H,Q^{\dagger}_{\nu\bm{q}}\right]=\hbar\omega_{\nu\bm{q}}Q^{\dagger}_{\nu\bm{q}}, (S31)

and it can be shown that, as a result, the following equation holds for any operator RR,

⟨0|[R,[H,Qν​𝒒†]]|0⟩=ων​𝒒​⟨0|[R,Qν​𝒒†]|0⟩.\matrixelement{0}{[R,[H,Q^\dagger_{\nu\boldsymbol{q}}]]}{0}=\omega_{\nu\bm{q}}\matrixelement{0}{[R,Q^\dagger_{\nu\boldsymbol{q}}]}{0}. (S32)

Taking R=Qν​𝒒R=Q_{\nu\bm{q}} and solving the equations of motion, one obtains the tdHF equations

∑𝒌(A𝒒​(𝒌′,𝒌)B𝒒​(𝒌′,𝒌)B−𝒒∗(𝒌′,𝒌)A−𝒒∗(𝒌′,𝒌))​(Xν​𝒒​(𝒌)Yν​𝒒​(𝒌))=ων​𝒒​(100−1)​(Xν​𝒒​(𝒌′)Yν​𝒒​(𝒌′)),\sum_{\bm{k}}\begin{pmatrix}A^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{k})&B^{\bm{q}}(\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{k})\\ B^{-\bm{q}*}(\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{k})&A^{-\bm{q}*}(\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{k})\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}X^{\nu\bm{q}}(\bm{k})\\ Y^{\nu\bm{q}}(\bm{k})\end{pmatrix}=\omega_{\nu\bm{q}}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}X^{\nu\bm{q}}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\\ Y^{\nu\bm{q}}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\end{pmatrix}, (S33)

where the particle-hole indices have been dropped for conciseness. Here ων​𝒒\omega_{\nu\bm{q}} are the energies of the excitations and the AA and BB matrices are defined as

A(φ′,φ)𝐪​(𝐤′,𝐤)=⟨H​F|[bφ′,𝐪​(𝐤′),[H,bφ,𝐪†​(𝐤)]]|H​F⟩A_{(\varphi^{\prime},\varphi)}^{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\mathbf{k})=\matrixelement{HF}{[b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\varphi',\vb{q}}(\vb{k}'), [H, b^\dagger_{\varphi,\vb{q}}(\vb{k})]]}{HF} (S34)

and

B(φ′,φ)𝐪​(𝐤′,𝐤)=−⟨H​F|[bφ′,𝐪​(𝐤′),[H,bφ,−𝐪​(𝐤)]]|H​F⟩.B_{(\varphi^{\prime},\varphi)}^{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}^{\prime},\mathbf{k})=-\matrixelement{HF}{[b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\varphi',\vb{q}}(\vb{k}'), [H, b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\varphi,-\vb{q}}(\vb{k})]]}{HF}. (S35)

Obtaining these equations involves taking the quasi-boson approximation, in which commutators of the particle-hole annihilation and creation operators are replaced by their expectation values taken in the HF ground state,

[bφ,𝒒​(𝒌),bφ′,𝒒†​(𝒌′)]≈⟨HF|[bφ,𝒒​(𝒌),bφ′,𝒒†​(𝒌′)]|HF⟩=δϕh​ϕh′​δϕp​ϕp′​δ​(𝒌−𝒌′)​δ​(𝒒−𝒒′).\left[b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\varphi,\bm{q}}(\bm{k}),b^{\dagger}_{\varphi^{\prime},\bm{q}}(\bm{k}^{\prime})\right]\approx\matrixelement{\text{HF}}{\left[b^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\varphi,\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}), b^\dagger_{\varphi',\boldsymbol{q}}(\boldsymbol{k}')\right]}{\text{HF}}=\delta_{\phi_{h}\phi_{h}^{\prime}}\delta_{\phi_{p}\phi_{p}^{\prime}}\delta(\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime})\delta(\bm{q}-\bm{q}^{\prime}). (S36)

It was recently shown that this approximation yields accurate correlation energies for the two-dimensional electron gas, so we expect it to perform well in this setting as well [65, 25].

Using the energies ων​𝒒\omega_{\nu\bm{q}} obtained by solving Eq. (S33), one can write down an effective bosonic Hamiltonian for the particle-hole excitations given by

HB=∑ν​𝐪ων​𝐪​Qν​𝐪†​Qν​𝐪+Ecorr.H_{\text{B}}=\sum_{\nu\mathbf{q}}\omega_{\nu\mathbf{q}}Q_{\nu\mathbf{q}}^{\dagger}Q_{\nu\mathbf{q}}+E_{\text{corr}}. (S37)

The correlation energy contributed by the zero-point motion of these collective modes is given by

Ecorr=12​∑ων​𝐪>0ων​𝐪−12​∑𝐪Tr​A𝐪,E_{\text{corr}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\omega_{\nu\mathbf{q}}>0}\omega_{\nu\mathbf{q}}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\text{Tr}A^{\mathbf{q}}, (S38)

where the first term is the sum of the energies of all the collective modes, and the second is the energies that the bare particle-hole excitations would have were the residual interactions between them not considered. This is the correlation energy we utilize in the main text.

It is important to consider how the correlation energy scales with both system size and the momentum cutoff. In Fig S6, we plot the correlation energy of the triangular lattice AHC with ℬ​A1BZ=2​π\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}=2\pi and Vc/Au.c.=2V_{c}/A_{\text{u.c.}}=2 as a function of n1n_{1} and nΓn_{\Gamma}. We find that the correlation energy scales as 1/n131/n_{1}^{3} with system size and converges exponentially with the number of reciprocal lattice vectors included. It is prohibitively expensive to converge the correlation energy well with respect to system size, so we must be careful interpreting the correlation energy stiff C66corr.C_{66}^{\text{corr.}}. In Fig. S7 we plot C66corr.C_{66}^{\text{corr.}} as a function of n1n_{1} and see that it scales like 1/n121/n_{1}^{2}. At n1=12n_{1}=12, the system size used to compute the stiffnesses in the main text, we see we have captured roughly 80% of the correlation energy stiffness, so our results are qualitatively unchanged by the finite system size and our conclusions hold.

IV Variational ansatz: perturbative energy calculation

Here we employ a variational ansatz for the parent band model that takes the form of a Slater determinant of single-particle states [56, 57],

|ψ𝒌𝒞⟩=𝒩𝒌​∑𝒈e−|𝒌+𝒈|24​ξ2−i​π​𝒞​[𝒌×𝒈A1​BZ+ω⁡(𝒈)]​ei⁡(𝒌+𝒈)⋅𝒓​|s𝒌+𝒈⟩,\ket{\psi^{\mathcal{C}}_{\bm{k}}}=\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}}\sum_{\bm{g}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{4\xi^{2}}-i\pi\mathcal{C}[\frac{\bm{k}\times\bm{g}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}+\omega(\bm{g})]}e^{i(\bm{k}+\bm{g})\cdot\bm{r}}\ket{s_{\bm{k}+\bm{g}}}, (S39)

where 𝒌\bm{k} is the crystal momentum, 𝒈\bm{g} enumerates the reciprocal lattice vectors, 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the Chern number, and A1BZA_{\text{1BZ}} is the area of the first Brillouin zone. Here ei​π​ω​(𝒈)e^{i\pi\omega(\bm{g})} is −1-1 if 𝒈/2\bm{g}/2 is a RLV and 11 otherwise, 𝒩𝒌\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}} is a normalization function, and ξ\xi is a variational parameter that controls the spread of the wavefunction in momentum space. For conciseness, we define the function

U𝒈​(𝐤)=e−|𝒌+𝒈|24​ξ2−i​π​𝒞​[𝒌×𝒈A1BZ+ω⁡(𝒈)]​ei⁡(𝒌+𝒈)⋅𝒓,U_{\bm{g}}(\mathbf{k})=e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{4\xi^{2}}-i\pi\mathcal{C}[\frac{\bm{k}\times\bm{g}}{A_{\text{1BZ}}}+\omega(\bm{g})]}e^{i(\bm{k}+\bm{g})\cdot\bm{r}}, (S40)

such that |ψ𝒌𝒞⟩=𝒩𝒌​∑𝒈U𝒈​(𝐤)​|s𝒌+𝒈⟩\ket{\psi^{\mathcal{C}}_{\bm{k}}}=\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}}\sum_{\bm{g}}U_{\bm{g}}(\mathbf{k})\ket{s_{\bm{k}+\bm{g}}} and |𝒩𝐤|−2=A​∑𝒈|U𝒈​(𝐤)|2|\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{k}}|^{-2}=A\sum_{\bm{g}}|U_{\bm{g}}(\mathbf{k})|^{2}, with AA the area of the sample.

We calculate the variational energy of the ansatz wavefunction by making a strong-interaction expansion. The authors of Refs. [57, 56] used this approach to estimate the energy, and we will follow their method closely. However, their zeroth-order result does not depend on the lattice and so carries no information about the mechanical properties of the anomalous Hall crystal. To approximate these quantities, we need the next terms in the strong-interaction expansion. Our main result for this section is an approximate expression for the total energy per particle of the anomalous Hall crystal state:

EN≈\displaystyle\frac{E}{N}\approx ξ2m−Vc4​α​π+12​ξ2m​∑shortest ​𝑹ξ2​|𝑹|2​e−ξ2​|𝑹|2\displaystyle\frac{\xi^{2}}{m}-\frac{V_{c}}{4\sqrt{\alpha\pi}}+\frac{1}{2}\frac{\xi^{2}}{m}\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}e^{-\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}
−Vc4​α​π∑shortest ​𝑹e−ξ2​|𝑹|2[3+e−|𝑹|22​αI0(|𝑹|22​α)−4e−|𝑹|28​αI0(|𝑹|28​α)],\displaystyle-\frac{V_{c}}{4\sqrt{\alpha\pi}}\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}\left[3+e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}}I_{0}\left(\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}\right)-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}}I_{0}\left(\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}\right)\right], (S41)

where I0I_{0} is the modified Bessel function of the first kind and α=1ξ2+4​𝒞​πA1​BZ\alpha=\frac{1}{\xi^{2}}+\frac{4\mathcal{C}\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}} with positive 𝒞\mathcal{C}. This expression holds when the Berry curvature of the parent band precisely matches the Chern number of the descendant band defined by the ansatz in Eq. (S39): ℬ​A1BZ/2​π=𝒞\mathcal{B}A_{\text{1BZ}}/2\pi=\mathcal{C}. Eq. (S41) gives a first-order expansion of the energy per particle, in the small parameter e−ξ2​a2e^{-\xi^{2}a^{2}}, where aa is the lattice constant of the crystal. This small parameter decreases with interaction strength for the optimized ansatz, as is known from the zeroth-order expansion [56, 57], so we expect the perturbative expression to be valid for large interaction strengths. Because the zeroth-order term does not depend on the lattice structure, any properties like stiffness will decay rapidly with interaction strength. In the first-order term, the energy depends on the lattice structure through the sum over the shortest lattice vectors 𝑹\bm{R}. When we compute the stiffness of the crystal, we must slightly deform the lattice, which changes the lattice vectors and results in a change in energy. We note that during this deformation, there will be lattice vectors that are very close in length to the shortest vectors. In this case, these vectors are also included in the sum.

In the remainder of this section, we explain how the energy is derived using a small-parameter expansion. We first examine the form factor for the descendant band, which is defined as

F⁡(𝒌+𝒒,𝒌)=⟨ψ⌈𝒌+𝒒⌉𝒞|ei​𝒒⋅𝒓|ψ𝒌𝒞⟩,F(\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k})=\braket{\psi_{\lceil\bm{k}+\bm{q}\rceil}^{\mathcal{C}}|e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}}|\psi_{\bm{k}}^{\mathcal{C}}}, (S42)

where ⌈𝒗⌉\lceil\bm{v}\rceil folds a vector 𝒗\bm{v} into the first Brillouin zone, and the states are in the descendant band defined by the ansatz (Eq. (S39)). Here 𝒌\bm{k} is in the first Brillouin zone, while 𝒒\bm{q} is a general momentum transfer. Defining 𝒈0=𝒌+𝒒−⌈𝒌+𝒒⌉\bm{g}_{0}=\bm{k}+\bm{q}-\lceil\bm{k}+\bm{q}\rceil, which is a reciprocal lattice vector (RLV), and η⁡(𝒈0)=ei​π​(ω⁡(𝒈0)−1)\eta(\bm{g}_{0})=e^{i\pi(\omega(\bm{g}_{0})-1)}, this form factor is given by [57]

F⁡(𝒌+𝒒,𝒌)=\displaystyle F(\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k})= A​𝒩𝒌+𝒒​𝒩𝒌​f​(𝒌)​e−(ℬ4+14​ξ2)​|𝒒|2​(η⁡(𝒈0))𝒞​ei​𝒞​π​(𝒌+𝒒)×𝒈0+𝒌×𝒒A1​BZ,\displaystyle A\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}}f(\bm{k})e^{-(\frac{\mathcal{B}}{4}+\frac{1}{4\xi^{2}})|\bm{q}|^{2}}(\eta(\bm{g}_{0}))^{\mathcal{C}}e^{i\mathcal{C}\pi\frac{(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\times\bm{g}_{0}+\bm{k}\times\bm{q}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}}, (S43)

for

f(𝒌)=∑𝒈e−iδ2𝒒×(𝒌+𝒈)e−|𝒌+𝒈|22​ξ2e−𝒒⋅(𝒌+𝒈)2​ξ2,\displaystyle f(\bm{k})=\sum_{\bm{g}}e^{-i\frac{\delta}{2}\bm{q}\times(\bm{k}+\bm{g})}e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2\xi^{2}}}e^{-\frac{\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{k}+\bm{g})}{2\xi^{2}}}, (S44)

where δ=ℬ−2​𝒞​πA1​BZ\delta=\mathcal{B}-\frac{2\mathcal{C}\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}. This can be cast into a form that converges more rapidly at large ξ\xi by taking a Fourier series expansion for f⁡(𝒌)f(\bm{k}), resulting in an expression in terms of a sum over lattice vectors 𝑹\bm{R} [57]:

f⁡(𝒌)=2​π​ξ2A1​BZ​e|𝒒|2​(1−δ2​ξ4)8​ξ2​∑𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹​eξ2​δ​𝑹×𝒒2.f(\bm{k})=\frac{2\pi\xi^{2}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}e^{\frac{|\bm{q}|^{2}(1-\delta^{2}\xi^{4})}{8\xi^{2}}}\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}}e^{\frac{\xi^{2}\delta\bm{R}\times\bm{q}}{2}}. (S45)

The form factor is then given by

F⁡(𝒌+𝒒,𝒌)=\displaystyle F(\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k})= A​2​π​ξ2A1​BZ​𝒩𝒌+𝒒​𝒩𝒌​(η⁡(𝒈0))𝒞​e−|𝒒|2​((1+δ​ξ2)28​ξ2+𝒞​π2​A1​BZ)​ei​𝒞​π​(𝒌+𝒒)×𝒈0+𝒌×𝒒A1​BZ​∑𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹​eξ2​δ​𝑹×𝒒2.\displaystyle A\frac{2\pi\xi^{2}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}}(\eta(\bm{g}_{0}))^{\mathcal{C}}e^{-|\bm{q}|^{2}(\frac{(1+\delta\xi^{2})^{2}}{8\xi^{2}}+\frac{\mathcal{C}\pi}{2A_{1\text{BZ}}})}e^{i\mathcal{C}\pi\frac{(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\times\bm{g}_{0}+\bm{k}\times\bm{q}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}}\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}}e^{\frac{\xi^{2}\delta\bm{R}\times\bm{q}}{2}}. (S46)

From now on, we will examine the case where δ=0\delta=0, meaning that the parent Berry flux through the Brillouin zone is equal to 2​π​𝒞2\pi\mathcal{C}. In this case

F⁡(𝒌+𝒒,𝒌)=\displaystyle F(\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k})= 2​π​ξ2​AA1​BZ​𝒩𝒌+𝒒​𝒩𝒌​(η⁡(𝒈0))𝒞​e−α​|𝒒|28​ei​𝒞​π​(𝒌+𝒒)×𝒈0+𝒌×𝒒A1​BZ​∑𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹.\displaystyle\frac{2\pi\xi^{2}A}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}}(\eta(\bm{g}_{0}))^{\mathcal{C}}e^{-\frac{\alpha|\bm{q}|^{2}}{8}}e^{i\mathcal{C}\pi\frac{(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\times\bm{g}_{0}+\bm{k}\times\bm{q}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}}\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}}. (S47)

The interaction energy for the many-body ansatz wavefunction is given in terms of the form factor as [57]

⟨Hint⟩\displaystyle\braket{H_{\text{int}}} =12​A​∑𝒌1,𝒌2∈BZ∑𝒒V⁡(−𝒒)​F​(𝒌1−𝒒,𝒌1)​F​(𝒌2+𝒒,𝒌2)​⟨c⌈𝒌1−𝒒⌉†​c⌈𝒌2+𝒒⌉†​c𝒌2​c𝒌1⟩D,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}\in\text{BZ}}\sum_{\bm{q}}V(-\bm{q})F(\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{q},\bm{k}_{1})F(\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{q},\bm{k}_{2})\braket{c_{\lceil\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{q}\rceil}^{\dagger}c_{\lceil\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{q}\rceil}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k}_{2}}c_{\bm{k}_{1}}}_{D}, (S48)

where the subscript DD on the expectation value indicates that the creation and annihilation operators belong to the descendant band. This energy can then be split into Hartree and Fock terms by noting that the expectation value is non-zero only when 𝒌2=⌈𝒌2+𝒒⌉\bm{k}_{2}=\lceil\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{q}\rceil (Hartree) or when 𝒌𝟐=⌈𝒌1−𝒒⌉\bm{k_{2}}=\lceil\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{q}\rceil (Fock), because the state is a Slater determinant. In the first case, 𝒒\bm{q} must be a RLV, which we denote by 𝒈\bm{g}. As a result, the interaction energy can be written as

⟨Hint⟩\displaystyle\braket{H_{\text{int}}} =12​A​∑𝒌1,𝒌2∈BZ∑𝒈V⁡(−𝒈)​F​(𝒌1−𝒈,𝒌1)​F​(𝒌2+𝒈,𝒌2)−12​A​∑𝒌1∈BZ∑𝒒V⁡(−𝒒)​|F⁡(𝒌1−𝒒,𝒌1)|2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}\in\text{BZ}}\sum_{\bm{g}}V(-\bm{g})F(\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{g},\bm{k}_{1})F(\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{g},\bm{k}_{2})-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{k}_{1}\in\text{BZ}}\sum_{\bm{q}}V(-\bm{q})|F(\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{q},\bm{k}_{1})|^{2} (S49)
=⟨HHartree⟩−⟨HFock⟩.\displaystyle=\braket{H_{\text{Hartree}}}-\braket{H_{\text{Fock}}}. (S50)

Following the approach used in Refs. [56, 57], we remove the long-ranged part of the Coulomb interaction by excluding 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 from the sum (and do the same for the sum over 𝒈\bm{g} in the Hartree term).

IV.1 Correction to the Fock term

We now compute approximations to the various terms in the variational energy, starting with the Fock term:

EFock\displaystyle E_{\text{Fock}} =−12​A∑𝒌∈BZ∑𝒒V(−𝒒)|F(𝒌−𝒒,𝒌)|2=−12​A∑𝒌∈BZ∑𝒒V(𝒒)|F(𝒌+𝒒,𝒌)|2.\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{k}\in\text{BZ}}\sum_{\bm{q}}V(-\bm{q})|F(\bm{k}-\bm{q},\bm{k})|^{2}=-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{k}\in\text{BZ}}\sum_{\bm{q}}V(\bm{q})|F(\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k})|^{2}.

We can substitute our expression for the form factors from Eq. (S47), to obtain

EFock\displaystyle E_{\text{Fock}} =−12​A∑𝒌∈BZ∑𝒒V(𝒒)(2​π​ξ2​AA1​BZ)2𝒩𝒌+𝒒2𝒩𝒌2e−α​|𝒒|24|∑𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ22ei⁡(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹|2.\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{k}\in\text{BZ}}\sum_{\bm{q}}V(\bm{q})\left(\frac{2\pi\xi^{2}A}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\right)^{2}\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}+\bm{q}}^{2}\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}}^{2}e^{-\frac{\alpha|\bm{q}|^{2}}{4}}\bigg|\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}}\bigg|^{2}.

The normalization factors can be written as a series that converges rapidly at large ξ\xi, using a Fourier expansion. We have

𝒩𝒌−2\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{\bm{k}}^{-2} =A​∑𝒈e−|𝒌+𝒈|22​ξ2=A​2​π​ξ2A1​BZ​∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22.\displaystyle=A\sum_{\bm{g}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2\xi^{2}}}=A\frac{2\pi\xi^{2}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}. (S51)

Using this expression, the Fock energy is given by

EFock\displaystyle E_{\text{Fock}} =−12​A∑𝒒V(𝒒)e−α​|𝒒|24∑𝒌∈BZ|∑𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹|2∑𝑹′ei​𝒌⋅𝑹′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′|22​∑𝑹′′ei⁡(𝒌+𝒒)⋅𝑹′′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′′|22.\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{q}}V(\bm{q})e^{-\frac{\alpha|\bm{q}|^{2}}{4}}\sum_{\bm{k}\in\text{BZ}}\frac{\bigg|\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}}\bigg|^{2}}{\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime}|^{2}}{2}}\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}}e^{i(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}|^{2}}{2}}}. (S52)

We are interested in the case where exp(−a2ξ2/2)≪1\exp(-a^2 \xi^2/2)\ll 1, where aa is the lattice constant (aa is the smaller lattice constant if the primitive lattice vectors have different lengths), which is realized in the strong interaction limit. exp(−a2ξ2/2)\exp(-a^2 \xi^2/2) then serves as a small parameter, allowing for a perturbative expansion. The zeroth-order term, which is computed in Ref. [57], can be found by taking 𝑹=𝑹′=𝑹′′=0\bm{R}=\bm{R}^{\prime}=\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}=0. To compute the first correction to the Fock energy, we first write

∑𝒌∈BZ|∑𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹|2∑𝑹′ei​𝒌⋅𝑹′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′|22​∑𝑹′′ei⁡(𝒌+𝒒)⋅𝑹′′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′′|22\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}\in\text{BZ}}\frac{\bigg|\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}}\bigg|^{2}}{\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime}|^{2}}{2}}\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}}e^{i(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}|^{2}}{2}}}
=∑𝒌∈BZ|1+∑𝑹≠0e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹|2(1+∑𝑹′≠0ei​𝒌⋅𝑹′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′|22)​(1+∑𝑹′′≠0ei⁡(𝒌+𝒒)⋅𝑹′′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′′|22)\displaystyle\hskip 113.81102pt=\sum_{\bm{k}\in\text{BZ}}\frac{\bigg|1+\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}}\bigg|^{2}}{\left(1+\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime}\neq 0}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime}|^{2}}{2}}\right)\left(1+\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}\neq 0}e^{i(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}|^{2}}{2}}\right)}

×[1−∑𝑹′≠0ei​𝒌⋅𝑹′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′|22+(∑𝑹′≠0ei​𝒌⋅𝑹′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′|22)2+…]\displaystyle\hskip 142.26378pt\times\left[1-\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime}\neq 0}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime}|^{2}}{2}}+\left(\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime}\neq 0}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime}|^{2}}{2}}\right)^{2}+...\right]
