At first, it may seem that the first correction will be a first-order term, which comes from taking the zeroth-order contribution from two of the terms in squared brackets and a first-order contribution from the remaining term. However, this is not the case. To see this, note that expanding the product gives an expression of the form

∑𝒌∈BZ\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}\in\text{BZ}} |∑𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹|2∑𝑹′ei​𝒌⋅𝑹′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′|22​∑𝑹′′ei⁡(𝒌+𝒒)⋅𝑹′′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′′|22\displaystyle\frac{\bigg|\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}}\bigg|^{2}}{\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime}|^{2}}{2}}\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}}e^{i(\bm{k}+\bm{q})\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime\prime}|^{2}}{2}}}
=∑𝒌(1+∑𝑹1≠0A1𝒒​(𝑹1)​e−|𝑹1|2​ξ22​ei​𝒌⋅𝑹1+∑𝑹1,𝑹2≠0A2𝒒​(𝑹1,𝑹2)​e−ξ22​(|𝑹1|2+|𝑹1|2)​ei​𝒌⋅(𝑹1+𝑹2)+…)\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}}\left(1+\sum_{\bm{R}_{1}\neq 0}A_{1}^{\bm{q}}(\bm{R}_{1})e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}_{1}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}_{1}}+\sum_{\bm{R}_{1},\bm{R}_{2}\neq 0}A_{2}^{\bm{q}}(\bm{R}_{1},\bm{R}_{2})e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}}{2}(|\bm{R}_{1}|^{2}+|\bm{R}_{1}|^{2})}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot(\bm{R}_{1}+\bm{R}_{2})}+...\right)
=∑𝒌(1+∑n=1∞∑{𝑹1,…,𝑹n≠0}An𝒒({𝑹1,…,𝑹n})e−ξ22∑i=1n|𝑹i|2ei​𝒌⋅∑i=1n𝑹i),\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}}\left(1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{\set{\bm{R}_{1},...,\bm{R}_{n}\neq 0}}A_{n}^{\bm{q}}(\set{\bm{R}_{1},...,\bm{R}_{n}})e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\bm{R}_{i}|^{2}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{R}_{i}}\right),

where the An𝒒A_{n}^{\bm{q}} are some functions that we have not yet computed, but which do not include the small parameter exp⁡(−a2​ξ2)\exp(-a^2\xi^2). The first-order terms are proportional to ∑𝒌ei​𝒌⋅𝑹\sum_{\bm{k}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}} for some non-zero lattice vector 𝑹\bm{R}. In the thermodynamic limit, this oscillatory term vanishes when summed over 𝒌\bm{k} if 𝑹\bm{R} is non-zero. Instead, the simplest contributing term is at second-order and involves two lattice vectors 𝑹1\bm{R}_{1} and 𝑹2\bm{R}_{2} such that 𝑹1+𝑹2=0\bm{R}_{1}+\bm{R}_{2}=0. More generally, we obtain contributions from the nnth order terms for which the sum of the nn lattice vectors is zero.

To determine the relative sizes of the different contributions, we examine the Gaussian factors. These decay exponentially with the sum of squared lengths of the lattice vectors. This means that the largest such term is a second-order term involving 𝑹1=−𝑹2\bm{R}_{1}=-\bm{R}_{2}, such that 𝑹1\bm{R}_{1} is one of the shortest lattice vectors (excluding the zero length one, which gives the zeroth-order contribution). In this case, the Gaussian factor is exp⁡(−a2​ξ2)\exp( - a^2 \xi^2), where aa is the lattice constant. The next largest terms, which we will not include, are either second-order contributions involving the second shortest lattice vectors or higher-order terms involving the shortest lattice vectors. Taking the square lattice as an example, both of these contributions are suppressed by the factor exp⁡(−2​a2​ξ2)\exp( - 2a^2 \xi^2), compared to the exp⁡(−a2​ξ2)\exp( - a^2 \xi^2) factor on the first contribution. This allows us to estimate when our leading term in the correction is sufficient to estimate the lattice-dependent component of the energy. We are using units where the length of the primitive RLV for the triangular lattice is unity. This means that the lattice constant for the square lattice of the same density is a=2​π​23a=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}}, meaning we need ξ>0.22\xi>0.22 or so for a correction of order 0.1, or ξ>0.32\xi>0.32 to get a correction of order 0.010.01. In the case of the triangular lattice, the next largest terms instead result from a third-order process involving three of the shortest lattice vectors, meaning that the term is suppressed by exp⁡(−32​a2​ξ2)\exp( - \frac{3}{2} a^2 \xi^2). With a=4​π3a=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}} for the triangular lattice, this term can be ignored compared to the first contribution when ξ>0.30\xi>0.30 (for a relative contribution of order 0.10.1) or ξ>0.42\xi>0.42 (for a relative contribution of order 0.010.01). Given that there will be more terms contributing at higher order, a larger ξ\xi may be required for good convergence. Note that this estimate for the convergence is in terms of the variational parameter ξ\xi rather than a physical parameter such as VcV_{c}. We discuss how the regime of applicability depends on the interaction strength, as well as the Chern number, in Sec. IV.4.

Having determined which terms to consider, we now compute the leading-order correction for the expression in Eq. (S53). We obtain one term by taking the second-order contribution from the first squared bracket and the zeroth-order contribution from the other brackets:

T1\displaystyle T_{1} =∑𝒌∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|22​ξ2ei⁡(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹∑shortest ​𝑹′e−|𝑹′|22​ξ2e−i(𝒒2+𝒌)⋅𝑹′δ𝑹,𝑹′=N∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2.\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}}\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}\xi^{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}}\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}^{\prime}|^{2}}{2}\xi^{2}}e^{-i(\frac{\bm{q}}{2}+\bm{k})\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime}}\delta_{\bm{R},\bm{R}^{\prime}}=N\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}.

We obtain a similar term by using the second-order contributions from the other two squared brackets instead:

T2\displaystyle T_{2} =2​N​∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2.\displaystyle=2N\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}.

Then, we have a cross term between the linear parts of the last two squared brackets

T3\displaystyle T_{3} =N∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2e−i𝒒⋅𝑹=N∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2cos⁡(𝒒⋅𝑹),\displaystyle=N\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{R}}=N\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}\cos(\boldsymbol{q} \cdot\boldsymbol{R}),

where we used inversion symmetry to take the real part of the exponential. Finally, we have a cross term between the linear part of the first squared bracket and the linear parts of the other two:

T4\displaystyle T_{4} =−2N∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2ei​𝒒⋅𝑹2(1+e−i𝒒⋅𝑹)=−4N∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2cos⁡(𝒒⋅𝑹2).\displaystyle=-2N\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}e^{i\frac{\bm{q}\cdot\bm{R}}{2}}(1+e^{-i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{R}})=-4N\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}\cos(\frac{\boldsymbol{q} \cdot\boldsymbol{R}}{2}).

Substituting these contributions, which approximate Eq. (S53), into the expression for the Fock energy given in Eq. (S52), we find

EFock\displaystyle E_{\text{Fock}} ≈−N2​A∑𝒒V(𝒒)e−α​|𝒒|24(1+∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2[3+cos⁡(𝒒⋅𝑹)−4cos⁡(𝒒⋅𝑹2)]).\displaystyle\approx-\frac{N}{2A}\sum_{\bm{q}}V(\bm{q})e^{-\frac{\alpha|\bm{q}|^{2}}{4}}\bigg(1+\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}\left[3+\cos(\boldsymbol{q} \cdot\boldsymbol{R})-4\cos(\frac{\boldsymbol{q} \cdot\boldsymbol{R}}{2})\right]\bigg). (S54)

Using the double-angle formula for cosine, we have

3+cos⁡(𝒒⋅𝑹)−4​cos⁡(𝒒⋅𝑹2)=2​(1−cos⁡(𝒒⋅𝑹2))2,3+\cos(\boldsymbol{q} \cdot\boldsymbol{R})-4\cos(\frac{\boldsymbol{q} \cdot\boldsymbol{R}}{2})=2\left(1-\cos(\frac{\boldsymbol{q} \cdot\boldsymbol{R}}{2})\right)^{2},

which is always non-negative, indicating that the correction enhances the magnitude of the Fock term.

In the infinite system size limit, we can convert the sum over 𝒒\bm{q} to an integral. We must be careful about 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0, which is excluded from the sum. This happens naturally in the integral, with the contribution from 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 vanishing. This is because the 1/|𝒒|1/|\bm{q}| factor from the Coulomb interaction cancels with a |𝒒||\bm{q}| factor in the integral measure in polar coordinates. The resulting integrand is non-divergent at the origin, and so the contribution from the single point at the origin is zero. We can therefore replace the sum over 𝒒≠0\bm{q}\neq 0 with an integral

∑𝒒≠0→A4​π2∫d2q=A4​π2∫dqdθq,\sum_{\bm{q}\neq 0}\rightarrow\frac{A}{4\pi^{2}}\int d^{2}q=\frac{A}{4\pi^{2}}\int dqd\theta q,

such that

EFock\displaystyle E_{\text{Fock}} ≈−N8​π2∫0∞dq∫02​πdθqV(q)e−α​q24(1+∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2[3+cos⁡(q​|𝑹|​cos⁡θ)−4cos⁡(q​|𝑹|​cos⁡θ2)]),\displaystyle\approx-\frac{N}{8\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dq\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta qV(q)e^{-\frac{\alpha q^{2}}{4}}\left(1+\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}\left[3+\cos(q|\boldsymbol{R}| \cos\theta)-4\cos(\frac{q|\boldsymbol{R}| \cos\theta}{2})\right]\right),

where we assume a rotationally symmetric interaction, and we align our axis with 𝑹\bm{R} for every term in the sum. Using the Coulomb interaction, V⁡(q)=Vc/qV(q)=V_{c}/q, we get

EFock\displaystyle E_{\text{Fock}} ≈−N8​π2∫0∞dq∫02​πdθVce−α​q24(1+∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2[3+cos⁡(q​|𝑹|​cos⁡θ)−4cos⁡(q​|𝑹|​cos⁡θ2)])\displaystyle\approx-\frac{N}{8\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dq\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta V_{c}e^{-\frac{\alpha q^{2}}{4}}\bigg(1+\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}\left[3+\cos(q|\boldsymbol{R}| \cos\theta)-4\cos(\frac{q|\boldsymbol{R}| \cos\theta}{2})\right]\bigg)
=EFock(0)+EFock(1).\displaystyle=E^{(0)}_{\text{Fock}}+E^{(1)}_{\text{Fock}}.

We first consider the zeroth-order term, which gives us

EFock(0)\displaystyle E_{\text{Fock}}^{(0)} =−N8​π2∫0∞dq∫02​πdθVce−α​q24=−N​Vc4​α​π.\displaystyle=-\frac{N}{8\pi^{2}}\int_{0}^{\infty}dq\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta V_{c}e^{-\frac{\alpha q^{2}}{4}}=-\frac{NV_{c}}{4\sqrt{\alpha\pi}}.

This agrees with the interaction term computed in Refs. [57, 56] for 𝒞=1\mathcal{C}=1 and δ=0\delta=0.

Next, we look at the first-order correction to the Fock energy. For the 3​e−|𝑹|2​ξ23e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}} term, there is no additional 𝒒\bm{q} dependence, so the integral immediately follows from the result above, giving the contribution

−3​N​Vc4​α​π∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2.-\frac{3NV_{c}}{4\sqrt{\alpha\pi}}\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}.

For the cosine terms in the correction, we must examine the integral

∫0∞d​q​e−14​α​q2​cos⁡(q​λ)=πα​e−λ2α,\int_{0}^{\infty}dq\ e^{-\frac{1}{4}\alpha q^{2}}\cos(q\lambda)=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}}e^{-\frac{\lambda^{2}}{\alpha}},

with λ=|𝑹|​cos⁡θ\lambda=|\bm{R}|\cos\theta or λ=(|𝑹|/2)​cos⁡θ\lambda=(|\bm{R}|/2)\cos\theta. Our first correction to the Fock term is

EFock(1)\displaystyle E_{\text{Fock}}^{(1)} =−3​N​Vc4​α​π∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2−N​Vc8​π2πα∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2∫02​πdθ(e−|𝑹|2​cos2​θα−4e−|𝑹|2​cos2​θ4​α).\displaystyle=-\frac{3NV_{c}}{4\sqrt{\alpha\pi}}\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}-\frac{NV_{c}}{8\pi^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}}\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\ \left(e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{\alpha}}-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{4\alpha}}\right).

Next, we use the double-angle formula to write cos2​θ=12​(cos⁡(2​θ)+1)\cos^{2}\theta=\frac{1}{2}(\cos(2\theta)+1). Then we swap the integration variable from θ\theta to ϕ=2​θ\phi=2\theta, obtaining

∫02​πd​θ​(e−|𝑹|2​cos2​θα−4​e−|𝑹|2​cos2​θ4​α)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\ \left(e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{\alpha}}-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{4\alpha}}\right) =12​∫04​πd​ϕ​(e−|𝑹|22​α​e−|𝑹|2​cos⁡ϕ2​α−4​e−|𝑹|28​α​e−|𝑹|2​cos⁡ϕ8​α)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{4\pi}d\phi\ \left(e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos\phi}{2\alpha}}-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos\phi}{8\alpha}}\right)
=∫02​πd​ϕ​(e−|𝑹|22​α​e−|𝑹|2​cos⁡ϕ2​α−4​e−|𝑹|28​α​e−|𝑹|2​cos⁡ϕ8​α)\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\phi\ \left(e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos\phi}{2\alpha}}-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos\phi}{8\alpha}}\right)
=2​∫π2​πd​ϕ​(e−|𝑹|22​α​e−|𝑹|2​cos⁡ϕ2​α−4​e−|𝑹|28​α​e−|𝑹|2​cos⁡ϕ8​α),\displaystyle=2\int_{\pi}^{2\pi}d\phi\ \left(e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos\phi}{2\alpha}}-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos\phi}{8\alpha}}\right),

where we used the fact that cos⁡ϕ\cos\phi is mirrored about ϕ=π\phi=\pi. Then we shift the integration variable by π\pi, resulting in a minus sign on the cosines, to get

∫02​πd​θ​(e−|𝑹|2​cos2​θα−4​e−|𝑹|2​cos2​θ4​α)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\ \left(e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{\alpha}}-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{4\alpha}}\right) =2​∫0πd​ϕ​(e−|𝑹|22​α​e+|𝑹|2​cos⁡ϕ2​α−4​e−|𝑹|28​α​e+|𝑹|2​cos⁡ϕ8​α).\displaystyle=2\int_{0}^{\pi}d\phi\ \left(e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}}e^{+\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos\phi}{2\alpha}}-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}}e^{+\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos\phi}{8\alpha}}\right).

This can be related to an integral representation of a Bessel function [3]

I0​(z)=1π​∫0πd​θ​ez​cos⁡θ,I_{0}(z)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta e^{z\cos\theta}, (S55)

where I0I_{0} is a modified Bessel function of the first kind. Therefore,

∫02​πd​θ​(e−|𝑹|2​cos2​θα−4​e−|𝑹|2​cos2​θ4​α)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\ \left(e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{\alpha}}-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\cos^{2}\theta}{4\alpha}}\right) =2​π​[e−|𝑹|22​α​I0​(|𝑹|22​α)−4​e−|𝑹|28​α​I0​(|𝑹|28​α)].\displaystyle=2\pi\left[e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}}I_{0}\left(\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}\right)-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}}I_{0}\left(\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}\right)\right].

As a result, the first correction to the Fock term is

EFock(1)\displaystyle E_{\text{Fock}}^{(1)} =−N​Vc4​α​π∑shortest ​𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ2[3+e−|𝑹|22​αI0(|𝑹|22​α)−4e−|𝑹|28​αI0(|𝑹|28​α)].\displaystyle=-\frac{NV_{c}}{4\sqrt{\alpha\pi}}\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}e^{-|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}\left[3+e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}}I_{0}\left(\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2\alpha}\right)-4e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}}I_{0}\left(\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}}{8\alpha}\right)\right]. (S56)

We note that the contribution from each lattice vector is heavily suppressed according to its length. Because of this, the Fock term will favor lattices with smaller lattice constants. As an example, the Fock term would favor the square lattice over the triangular lattice and would also promote lattices where the primitive lattice vectors have different lengths. However, as we shall see in the next section, this effect is countered by the kinetic term.

IV.2 Correction to kinetic term

The other significant contribution to the energy comes from the kinetic term. Refs. [56, 57] also give an expression for this contribution in the strong-interaction limit. Once again, they restrict to the leading-order term, which is independent of the AHC lattice. In this section, we calculate the next contribution to determine the effect of the lattice shape. Using the quadratic dispersion of the parent band, the expectation value of the kinetic energy for the 𝒌\bm{k} ansatz state is

E⁡(𝒌)\displaystyle E(\bm{k}) =∑𝒈|𝒌+𝒈|22​m​e−|𝒌+𝒈|22​ξ2∑𝒈e−|𝒌+𝒈|22​ξ2.\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\bm{g}}\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2m}e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2\xi^{2}}}}{\sum_{\bm{g}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2\xi^{2}}}}. (S57)

We can gain some intuition about how the kinetic energy depends on the lattice by considering the weak-interaction limit, where ξ\xi is very small. In this case, the Gaussian factor ensures that the ansatz state at crystal momentum 𝒌\bm{k} is comprised almost entirely of the parent band state at 𝒌+𝒈\bm{k}+\bm{g} such that |𝒌+𝒈||\bm{k}+\bm{g}| is minimized. This results in significant occupation of states only in the Wigner-Seitz cell version of the Brillouin zone, with the total kinetic energy being the sum of the dispersion over the Wigner-Seitz cell (because the parent band states with a given crystal momentum after band-folding must have a total occupation of one). A Wigner-Seitz cell with a smaller average |𝒌+𝒈|2|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2} will have lower kinetic energy, meaning that a lattice with a nearly circular Wigner-Seitz cell would be preferred. This favors the triangular lattice, which has a hexagonal cell, over the square lattice, which has a square cell. It also disfavors dilation, increasing the energy of the rectangular lattice over the square lattice. This rule is a general one since it does not depend on the Berry curvature or band geometry of the parent band, although it could be affected by the dispersion.

Although this effect is most pronounced for low ξ\xi, we are more interested in the high ξ\xi limit. To access this, we perform the same Poisson summation that we employed for the Fock term. Firstly, from Eq. (S51) we know that

∑𝒈e−|𝒌+𝒈|22​ξ2=2​π​ξ2A1​BZ​∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22.\sum_{\bm{g}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2\xi^{2}}}=\frac{2\pi\xi^{2}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}.

We can then obtain ∑𝒈|𝒌+𝒈|22​m​e−|𝒌+𝒈|22​ξ2\sum_{\bm{g}}\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2m}e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2\xi^{2}}} from this expression by taking a derivative with respect to 1ξ2\frac{1}{\xi^{2}} on both sides:

dd⁡(1/ξ2)​∑𝒈e−|𝒌+𝒈|22​ξ2=dd⁡(1/ξ2)​2​π​ξ2A1​BZ​∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22\displaystyle\frac{d}{d(1/\xi^{2})}\sum_{\bm{g}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2\xi^{2}}}=\frac{d}{d(1/\xi^{2})}\frac{2\pi\xi^{2}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}
⟹|𝒌+𝒈|22​m​e−|𝒌+𝒈|22​ξ2=2​π​ξ4m​A1​BZ​∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22​(1−ξ2​|𝑹|22).\displaystyle\implies\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2m}e^{-\frac{|\bm{k}+\bm{g}|^{2}}{2\xi^{2}}}=\frac{2\pi\xi^{4}}{mA_{1\text{BZ}}}\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}\left(1-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}\right).

Therefore, the kinetic energy of a single electron is given by

E⁡(𝒌)\displaystyle E(\bm{k}) =ξ2m​∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22​(1−ξ2​|𝑹|22)∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22=ξ2m​(1−∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22​ξ2​|𝑹|22∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22).\displaystyle=\frac{\xi^{2}}{m}\frac{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}\left(1-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}\right)}{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}}=\frac{\xi^{2}}{m}\left(1-\frac{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}}\right). (S58)

The zeroth-order term is ξ2/m\xi^{2}/m, which is independent of 𝒌\bm{k} and agrees with the result from Ref. [56]. Now, we wish to compute the correction to the total kinetic energy

Ekin.=∑𝒌E⁡(𝒌)=∑𝒌ξ2m​(1−∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22​ξ2​|𝑹|22∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22).E_{\text{kin.}}=\sum_{\bm{k}}E(\bm{k})=\sum_{\bm{k}}\frac{\xi^{2}}{m}\left(1-\frac{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}}\right). (S59)

It is important to include the sum over 𝒌\bm{k} before we do the expansion. This is because, just as we saw for the Fock term, the first-order term would look like ei​𝒌⋅𝑹e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}, but this is destroyed by the sum over 𝒌\bm{k} unless 𝑹=0\bm{R}=0. This means that the leading contribution to the correction will actually come from the second-order terms. We start by writing

∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22​ξ2​|𝑹|22∑𝑹ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}} =∑𝑹≠0ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22​ξ2​|𝑹|221+∑𝑹≠0ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}{1+\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}}
≈∑𝑹≠0ei​𝒌⋅𝑹​e−ξ2​|𝑹|22​ξ2​|𝑹|22​[1−∑𝑹′≠0ei​𝒌⋅𝑹′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′|22+(∑𝑹′≠0ei​𝒌⋅𝑹′​e−ξ2​|𝑹′|22)2+…].\displaystyle\approx\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}}\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}{2}\left[1-\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime}\neq 0}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime}|^{2}}{2}}+\left(\sum_{\bm{R}^{\prime}\neq 0}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}^{\prime}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}|\bm{R}^{\prime}|^{2}}{2}}\right)^{2}+...\right].

Requiring the oscillatory component to vanish, the first contribution must involve 𝑹=−𝑹′\bm{R}=-\bm{R^{\prime}}, with 𝑹\bm{R} among the shortest lattice vectors. This term is of order ξ2​a2​e−ξ2​a2\xi^{2}a^{2}e^{-\xi^{2}a^{2}}, where aa is the lattice constant. For the square lattice, the next term comes either from including the next-shortest lattice vectors, with length 2​a\sqrt{2}a, or by taking the fourth-order term involving only the shortest lattice vectors. The next term is of order 4​ξ2​a2​e−2​ξ2​a24\xi^{2}a^{2}e^{-2\xi^{2}a^{2}}, so the realm of applicability is determined by 4​e−ξ2​a24e^{-\xi^{2}a^{2}}. The exponential decay of this next term is the same as for the Fock term, although the |𝑹|2|\bm{R}|^{2} factor in front of the expression for the kinetic term correction slows the decay with |𝑹||\bm{R}|. This means that the region of applicability for our expansion likely starts at slightly higher ξ\xi than for the Fock term correction.

Using the smallest term, with 𝑹=−𝑹′\bm{R}=-\bm{R}^{\prime} so that it contributes after the sum over 𝒌\bm{k}, we get

Ekin.≈N​ξ2m+N​ξ42​m​∑shortest ​𝑹|𝑹|2​e−ξ2​|𝑹|2=Ekin.(0)+Ekin.(1).E_{\text{kin.}}\approx N\frac{\xi^{2}}{m}+N\frac{\xi^{4}}{2m}\sum_{\text{shortest }\bm{R}}|\bm{R}|^{2}e^{-\xi^{2}|\bm{R}|^{2}}=E^{(0)}_{\text{kin.}}+E^{(1)}_{\text{kin.}}. (S60)

We see that this correction gives an energetic cost to smaller |𝑹||\bm{R}|, which disfavors the square lattice compared to the triangular lattice. This behavior is opposite to the Fock term, so the two energetic terms compete.

IV.3 Hartree term

Unlike for the kinetic and Fock terms, Refs. [56, 57] do not give an explicit expression for the Hartree term. This is because it is heavily suppressed compared to the other terms. However, the Hartree term may be significant compared to the corrections to the other terms that we have considered so far. In this section, we will show that the Hartree term is negligible even in this context. The Hartree term is given by

⟨HHartree⟩\displaystyle\braket{H_{\text{Hartree}}} =12​A​∑𝒌1,𝒌2∈BZ∑𝒈≠0V⁡(−𝒈)​F​(𝒌1−𝒈,𝒌1)​F​(𝒌2+𝒈,𝒌2).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}\in\text{BZ}}\sum_{\bm{g}\neq 0}V(-\bm{g})F(\bm{k}_{1}-\bm{g},\bm{k}_{1})F(\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{g},\bm{k}_{2}). (S61)

Using our expression for the form factor (Eq. (S47)), we have

F⁡(𝒌2+𝒈,𝒌2)=\displaystyle F(\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{g},\bm{k}_{2})= (η⁡(𝒈))𝒞​e−α​|𝒈|28​e2​i​𝒞​π​𝒌2×𝒈A1​BZ​∑𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒈2+𝒌2)⋅𝑹∑𝑹e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei​𝒌2⋅𝑹,\displaystyle(\eta(\bm{g}))^{\mathcal{C}}e^{-\frac{\alpha|\bm{g}|^{2}}{8}}e^{2i\mathcal{C}\pi\frac{\bm{k}_{2}\times\bm{g}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}}\frac{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{g}}{2}+\bm{k}_{2})\cdot\bm{R}}}{\sum_{\bm{R}}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\bm{k}_{2}\cdot\bm{R}}},

where we used 𝒒=𝒈\bm{q}=\bm{g} and 𝒈0​(𝒌2+𝒈)=𝒈\bm{g}_{0}(\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{g})=\bm{g}.

Because the only place 𝒌2\bm{k}_{2} enters the Hartree term is in this form factor, we can sum over 𝒌2\bm{k}_{2} in the Brillouin zone here. This looks quite similar to the expression we had for the Fock term, and we can expand it in a similar way. However, whereas for the Fock term we needed our expansion over the 𝑹\bm{R} to have no net oscillatory term, in this case, we have an oscillatory pre-factor exp⁡(2​i​𝒞​π​𝒌2×𝒈A1​BZ)\exp(2i \mathcal{C} \pi\frac{\boldsymbol{k}_2 \times\boldsymbol{g} }{A_{1\text{BZ}}}) which must be canceled out. This means that we get a large decay factor from the 𝑹\bm{R} terms when 𝒈\bm{g} is large, as well as the existing prefactor (for 𝒞≠0\mathcal{C}\neq 0). This results in the Hartree term being very heavily suppressed, even compared to the correction to the Fock term. This is even more pronounced for higher 𝒞\mathcal{C} because the required oscillatory component becomes a larger lattice vector.

The largest contribution will come from the smallest reciprocal lattice vectors 𝒈\bm{g} (note that we exclude 𝒈=0\bm{g}=0, which corresponds to the long-ranged component of the Coulomb force). We start by expanding:

∑𝒌2F⁡(𝒌2+𝒈,𝒌2)\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{k}_{2}}F(\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{g},\bm{k}_{2}) =(η⁡(𝒈))𝒞​e−α​|𝒈|28​∑𝒌2e2​i​𝒞​π​𝒌2×𝒈A1​BZ​(1+∑𝑹≠0e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒈2+𝒌2)⋅𝑹)\displaystyle=(\eta(\bm{g}))^{\mathcal{C}}e^{-\frac{\alpha|\bm{g}|^{2}}{8}}\sum_{\bm{k}_{2}}e^{2i\mathcal{C}\pi\frac{\bm{k}_{2}\times\bm{g}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}}\left(1+\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{g}}{2}+\bm{k}_{2})\cdot\bm{R}}\right)
×[1−∑𝑹≠0e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei​𝒌2⋅𝑹+(∑𝑹≠0e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei​𝒌2⋅𝑹)2+…].\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\times\left[1-\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\bm{k}_{2}\cdot\bm{R}}+\left(\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\bm{k}_{2}\cdot\bm{R}}\right)^{2}+...\right].

We consider the term involving the 1 in the first bracket:

S1:=∑𝒌2e2​i​𝒞​π​𝒌2×𝒈A1​BZ​[1−∑𝑹≠0e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei​𝒌2⋅𝑹+(∑𝑹≠0e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei​𝒌2⋅𝑹)2+…].\displaystyle S_{1}:=\sum_{\bm{k}_{2}}e^{2i\mathcal{C}\pi\frac{\bm{k}_{2}\times\bm{g}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}}\left[1-\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\bm{k}_{2}\cdot\bm{R}}+\left(\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\bm{k}_{2}\cdot\bm{R}}\right)^{2}+...\right].

We can write this as

S1\displaystyle S_{1} =∑𝒌2e2​i​𝒞​π​𝒌2×𝒈A1​BZ∑n=0∞(−1)n∑𝑹1,..𝑹ne−∑j=1n|𝑹j|2​ξ22ei​𝒌2⋅∑j=1n𝑹jδ(∑j𝑹j,−2𝒞πA1​BZ𝜺𝒈),\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}_{2}}e^{2i\mathcal{C}\pi\frac{\bm{k}_{2}\times\bm{g}}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\sum_{\bm{R}_{1},..\bm{R}_{n}}e^{-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{|\bm{R}_{j}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\bm{k}_{2}\cdot\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{R}_{j}}\delta\left(\sum_{j}\bm{R}_{j},-2\mathcal{C}\frac{\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{g}\right),

where 𝜺\bm{\varepsilon} is the unit antisymmetric matrix and the Kronecker delta is from the requirement that the overall oscillatory component be trivial for the sum over 𝒌\bm{k} to be nonzero. Note that 2​𝒞​πA1​BZ​𝜺​𝒈2\mathcal{C}\frac{\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{g} is always a lattice vector. Indeed f⁡(𝒈)=2​πA1​BZ​𝜺​𝒈f(\bm{g})=\frac{2\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{g} defines an invertible map from the reciprocal lattice to the direct lattice, with f−1​(𝒂)=−A1​BZ2​π​𝜺​𝒂f^{-1}(\bm{a})=-\frac{A_{1\text{BZ}}}{2\pi}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{a}. As a result, 2​𝒞​πA1​BZ​𝜺​𝒈2\mathcal{C}\frac{\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{g} is a lattice vector with minimum length 𝒞​a\mathcal{C}a, where aa is the lattice constant. Then

S1\displaystyle S_{1} =∑𝒌2∑n=0∞(−1)n∑𝑹1,..𝑹ne−∑j=1n|𝑹j|2​ξ22δ(∑j𝑹j,−2𝒞πA1​BZ𝜺𝒈).\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}_{2}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\sum_{\bm{R}_{1},..\bm{R}_{n}}e^{-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{|\bm{R}_{j}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}\delta\left(\sum_{j}\bm{R}_{j},-2\mathcal{C}\frac{\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{g}\right).

We can think of this as a weighted sum over paths made from lattice vectors, with the Kronecker delta enforcing that the end-point of the path is −2​𝒞​πA1​BZ​𝜺​𝒈.-2\mathcal{C}\frac{\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{g}. The weight depends on the sum of squared lengths for the segments. Because of this, the weight is higher if we take many small steps rather than a single segment that reaches the end-point. For general 𝒈\bm{g}, we may need to consider many different paths with the same weight. However, the situation is simpler when we consider only 𝒈\bm{g} that are among the shortest reciprocal lattice vectors. Consider first the square lattice. Then the shortest RLV are 2​πa​(±1,0)\frac{2\pi}{a}(\pm 1,0) and 2​πa​(0,±1)\frac{2\pi}{a}(0,\pm 1), where aa is the lattice constant. Taking 𝑮1=2​πa​(1,0)\bm{G}_{1}=\frac{2\pi}{a}(1,0) as an example, we have

−2​𝒞​πA1​BZ​𝜺​𝑮1\displaystyle-2\mathcal{C}\frac{\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{G}_{1} =−𝒞​4​π2a​A1​BZ​(01−10)​(10)=(0𝒞​a),\displaystyle=-\mathcal{C}\frac{4\pi^{2}}{aA_{1\text{BZ}}}\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ \mathcal{C}a\end{pmatrix},

where we used the fact that the Brillouin zone area is just 4​π2a2\frac{4\pi^{2}}{a^{2}} for a square lattice. We see that this is along one of the primitive lattice directions, with a length of 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

For a more general lattice, it is still true that if 𝒈\bm{g} is one of the shortest reciprocal lattice vectors, then f⁡(𝒈)=2​πA1​BZ​𝜺​𝒈f(\bm{g})=\frac{2\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{g} is one of the shortest lattice vectors. This is because the invertible map f⁡(𝒈)f(\bm{g}) gives a lattice vector with length proportional to |𝒈||\bm{g}|, so the shortest reciprocal lattice vectors give the shortest lattice vectors (and the map is invertible, so all lattice vectors are reached by the map). As a result, −2​𝒞​πA1​BZ​𝜺​𝒈-\frac{2\mathcal{C}\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\bm{\varepsilon}\bm{g} is parallel to one of the shortest lattice vectors, 𝑨\bm{A}, but with length equal to 𝒞\mathcal{C} times the length aa of that vector. The highest weighted path that reaches this vector is then made from 𝒞\mathcal{C} copies of 𝑨\bm{A}, with the sum of squared lengths equal to 𝒞​a2\mathcal{C}a^{2}. The Gaussian factor attached to this path is then exp⁡(−𝒞​a2​ξ22)\exp(-\frac{\mathcal{C}a^2 \xi^2}{2}). If 𝒞>1\mathcal{C}>1, this is significantly better than the term involving only one vector, which would have a sum of squared lengths 𝒞2​a2\mathcal{C}^{2}a^{2}. Only including the largest term for 𝒈\bm{g}, we get the approximation for S1S_{1} as

S1≈N​(−1)𝒞​e−𝒞​a2​ξ22S_{1}\approx N(-1)^{\mathcal{C}}e^{-\frac{\mathcal{C}a^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}} (S62)

Next, we consider the term involving the other part of the numerator:

S2\displaystyle S_{2} =∑𝒌2∑𝑹≠0e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei⁡(𝒈2+𝒌2)⋅𝑹​[1−∑𝑹≠0e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei​𝒌2⋅𝑹+(∑𝑹≠0e−|𝑹|2​ξ22​ei​𝒌2⋅𝑹)2+…]\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{k}_{2}}\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i(\frac{\bm{g}}{2}+\bm{k}_{2})\cdot\bm{R}}\left[1-\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\bm{k}_{2}\cdot\bm{R}}+\left(\sum_{\bm{R}\neq 0}e^{-\frac{|\bm{R}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\bm{k}_{2}\cdot\bm{R}}\right)^{2}+...\right]
=∑n=1∞(−1)n−1∑𝑹1,..𝑹ne−∑j=1n|𝑹j|2​ξ22ei​𝒈2⋅𝑹1δ(∑j𝑹j,−2𝒞πA1​BZϵ𝒈).\displaystyle=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}\sum_{\bm{R}_{1},..\bm{R}_{n}}e^{-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{|\bm{R}_{j}|^{2}\xi^{2}}{2}}e^{i\frac{\bm{g}}{2}\cdot\bm{R}_{1}}\delta\left(\sum_{j}\bm{R}_{j},-2\mathcal{C}\frac{\pi}{A_{1\text{BZ}}}\epsilon\bm{g}\right).

The same logic as before applies. This time, we have the phase factor exp⁡(i​𝒈2⋅𝑹1)\exp(i \frac{\boldsymbol{g}}{2} \cdot\boldsymbol{R}_1). In our leading term, 𝑹1\bm{R}_{1} is orthogonal to 𝒈\bm{g}, so the phase factor is 1. Then, because we have (−1)n−1(-1)^{n-1} rather than (−1)n(-1)^{n}, this cancels with the leading term from S1S_{1} giving us zero. As a result, S1+S2S_{1}+S_{2} decays faster than exp⁡(−𝒞​a2​ξ22)\exp(-\frac{\mathcal{C}a^2 \xi^2}{2}). The Hartree term, which includes two copies of the form factor (one for 𝒌1\bm{k}_{1} and one for 𝒌2\bm{k}_{2}), therefore decays faster than exp⁡(−𝒞​a2​ξ2)\exp(-\mathcal{C}a^2 \xi^2) even before we consider the other factors. Therefore, it decays faster than the first corrections to the Fock and kinetic terms and should only be included if further corrections to those terms are also used.

IV.4 Convergence of the perturbative expansion

In this section, we discuss the convergence of the perturbative expansion in slightly more detail. We estimated that the general region of convergence for the triangular lattice should be ξ>0.42\xi>0.42, which we round up to ξ>0.45\xi>0.45. We can check this rough estimate by using the kinetic energy for the triangular lattice, which we expect to have the slowest convergence of the terms that we have considered so far. The kinetic energy can be calculated numerically for large system sizes and large cutoffs. By comparing the difference between this value, Ekin.FSE^{\text{FS}}_{\text{kin.}} and the perturbative calculation Ekin.(0)+Ekin.(1)E^{(0)}_{\text{kin.}}+E^{(1)}_{\text{kin.}}, then dividing it by the first-order correction Ekin.(1)E^{(1)}_{\text{kin.}} in the perturbative calculation, we can estimate the relative strength of the uncalculated higher order terms in the perturbative expansion. We compare the strength of these terms to the first correction rather than the entire kinetic energy because the zeroth-order contribution does not depend on the lattice. Accordingly, it does not affect quantities like the stiffness. As shown in Fig. S8a, the untreated terms are of the order 0.01 compared to the first correction above ξ≈0.45\xi\approx 0.45, roughly agreeing with our previous estimate.

So far, we have estimated when the perturbative expansion should work well in terms of the variational parameter. However, we should also know what values of interaction strength this corresponds to. In Fig. S8b, we plot the optimized variational parameter as a function of VcV_{c} for different values of the Berry curvature and compare this to ξc=0.45\xi_{c}=0.45, above which we expect the leading-order expansion to be accurate. As we see from the plot, the expansion should work well for ℬ​A1​BZ=2​π\mathcal{B}A_{1\text{BZ}}=2\pi for all interaction strengths that we consider. On the other hand, the expansion is only likely to give highly accurate answers for ℬ​A1​BZ=4​π\mathcal{B}A_{1\text{BZ}}=4\pi above Vc/Au.c≈5V_{c}/A_{\text{u.c}}\approx 5 and for ℬ​A1​BZ=6​π\mathcal{B}A_{1\text{BZ}}=6\pi above Vc/Au.c≈8.5V_{c}/A_{\text{u.c}}\approx 8.5.

V Variation of the kinetic energy with a Mexican hat dispersion

In the main text, we have mentioned that having a dispersion with a minimum at a finite momentum |𝒌|=k0|\bm{k}|=k_{0} as

ℰ⁡(𝒌)=D⁡((|𝒌|k0)4−(|𝒌|k0)2)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(\bm{k})=D\left(\left(\frac{|\bm{k}|}{k_{0}}\right)^{4}-\left(\frac{|\bm{k}|}{k_{0}}\right)^{2}\right) (S63)

may lead to a mechanical instability of the triangular lattice electronic crystal. Indeed, if the minimum k0k_{0} sits just outside of the first Brillouin zone, the electronic crystal can reduce its kinetic energy by distorting the triangular lattice to more significantly occupy the states with low kinetic energy.

To substantiate this idea, we show in Fig. S9 the variation of the kinetic energy for distorted crystals as a function of udu_{d}. We assume that we have a single electron per crystal momentum 𝒌\bm{k} in the first BZ that occupies the lowest kinetic energy state, such that

Ekin=∫1BZd2​k​min𝒈​[ℰ⁡(𝒌+𝒈)].\displaystyle E_{\text{kin}}=\int_{\text{1BZ}}d^{2}k\min_{\bm{g}}\left[\mathcal{E}(\bm{k}+\bm{g})\right]. (S64)

Taking the the shortest reciprocal lattice vectors to have unit length |𝑮1,2|=1|\bm{G}_{1,2}|=1 for ud=0u_{d}=0, we see in Fig. S9 that if the minimum of the dispersion sits inside the first Brillouin zone (e.g., k0=0.45k_{0}=0.45), the kinetic energy of the crystal is minimized for a triangular lattice (ud=0u_{d}=0). In contrast, if we have a dispersion minimum that sits just outside the first Brillouin zone (e.g., k0=0.6k_{0}=0.6 as in the main text), the crystal can reduce its kinetic energy by distorting the triangular lattice to more significantly occupy states with small dispersion. As argued in the main text, it is exactly this reduction of the kinetic energy that is driving the mechanical instability of the AHC with the Mexican hat dispersion and in R5G for a strong displacement field.

VI Rhombohedral pentalayer graphene

For pentalayer rhombohedral graphene, we follow the modeling used in Ref. [15]. For this work to be self-contained, we briefly review and summarize the construction below.

VI.1 Microscopic model

VI.1.1 Moiré lattice

The initial graphene reciprocal lattice basis vectors are

𝑮1\displaystyle\bm{G}_{1} =4​π3​aG​(0,1)\displaystyle=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}a_{\text{G}}}\left(0,1\right) (S65a)
𝑮2\displaystyle\bm{G}_{2} =4​π3​aG​(−3,1).\displaystyle=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}a_{\text{G}}}\left(-\sqrt{3},1\right). (S65b)

The associated real space basis vectors respect 𝑨i⋅𝑮j=2​π​δi​j\bm{A}_{i}\cdot\bm{G}_{j}=2\pi\delta_{ij}. The real space basis vectors of the hBN substrate are obtained as

𝑨j′=M​R​[θ]​𝑨j;M=11+ε​I,\displaystyle\bm{A}_{j}^{\prime}=MR[\theta]\bm{A}_{j};\quad M=\frac{1}{1+\varepsilon}I, (S66)

where R⁡[θ]R[\theta] is a counter-clockwise rotation matrix and ε=(aG/ahBN−1)≈−0.01698\varepsilon=(a_{\text{G}}/a_{\text{hBN}}-1)\approx-0.01698 is the lattice mismatch. We note that the lattice constants of monolayer graphene and hBN are aG=0.246​nma_{\text{G}}=0.246\mathrm{~nm} and ahBN=0.25025​nma_{\text{hBN}}=0.25025\mathrm{~nm}, respectively.

The moiré reciprocal lattice vectors obtained by stacking graphene on top of hBN with a twist angle θ\theta are

𝑮imBZ=𝑮i−𝑮i′=(1−M−1​R​[θ])​𝑮i≈ε​𝑮i−θ​z^×𝑮i,\displaystyle\bm{G}_{i}^{\text{mBZ}}=\bm{G}_{i}-\bm{G}_{i}^{\prime}=(1-M^{-1}R[\theta])\bm{G}_{i}\approx\varepsilon\bm{G}_{i}-\theta\hat{z}\crossproduct\bm{G}_{i}, (S67)

where the approximation holds for small twist angle and lattice mismatch. It is also convenient to define the reciprocal lattice vector 𝑮3mBZ=𝑮2mBZ−𝑮1mBZ\bm{G}_{3}^{\text{mBZ}}=\bm{G}_{2}^{\text{mBZ}}-\bm{G}_{1}^{\text{mBZ}}, 𝑮4mBZ=−𝑮1mBZ\bm{G}_{4}^{\text{mBZ}}=-\bm{G}_{1}^{\text{mBZ}}, 𝑮5mBZ=−𝑮2mBZ\bm{G}_{5}^{\text{mBZ}}=-\bm{G}_{2}^{\text{mBZ}}, and 𝑮6mBZ=−𝑮3mBZ\bm{G}_{6}^{\text{mBZ}}=-\bm{G}_{3}^{\text{mBZ}}. The twist angle of 0.77∘0.77^{\circ} reported in experiments [38], leads to a moiré lattice constant of λM=|𝑨imBZ|≈aG/ε2+θ2≈11.4​nm\lambda_{M}=|\bm{A}_{i}^{\text{mBZ}}|\approx a_{\text{G}}/\sqrt{\varepsilon^{2}+\theta^{2}}\approx 11.4\mathrm{~nm}.

VI.1.2 Moiré rhombohedral graphene Hamiltonian

The moiré rhombohedral graphene Hamiltonian is

H=HR5G+HM+HC,\displaystyle H=H_{\text{R5G}}+H_{M}+H_{C}, (S68)

where HR5GH_{\text{R5G}} is the continuum kinetic term, HMH_{M} the moiré potential from the hBN substrate that is acting on the bottom graphene layer, and HCH_{C} the Coulomb potential. The continuum kinetic term is obtained by expanding the rhombohedral pentalayer graphene Hamiltonian about the 𝑲\bm{K} and 𝑲′\bm{K}^{\prime} valleys

VI.1.3 Band basis

Due to the large number of bands (coming from the sublattices, layers, and reciprocal lattice vectors within the momentum cutoff considered), the Hartree-Fock calculation will be done by only considering the nbandsn_{\text{bands}} lowest conduction bands [15, 33, 13, 74, 18]. To do so, it is first convenient to work in a band basis obtained by diagonalizing the quadratic part of the Hamiltonian

HKin\displaystyle H_{\text{Kin}} =HR5G+HM=∑𝒌∑η,σc𝒌,𝒈​α​ℓ​η​σ†​[hKinη​(𝒌)](𝒈​α​ℓ),(𝒈′​β​ℓ′)​c𝒌,𝒈′​β​ℓ′​η​σ,\displaystyle=H_{\text{R5G}}+H_{M}=\sum_{\bm{k}}\sum_{\eta,\sigma}c_{\bm{k},\bm{g}\alpha\ell\eta\sigma}^{\dagger}[h_{\text{Kin}}^{\eta}(\bm{k})]_{(\bm{g}\alpha\ell),(\bm{g}^{\prime}\beta\ell^{\prime})}c_{\bm{k},\bm{g}^{\prime}\beta\ell^{\prime}\eta\sigma}, (S82)

where c𝒌+𝒈,α​ℓ​η​σ≡c𝒌,𝒈​α​ℓ​η​σc_{\bm{k}+\bm{g},\alpha\ell\eta\sigma}\equiv c_{\bm{k},\bm{g}\alpha\ell\eta\sigma} with 𝒈=m​𝑮1mBZ+n​𝑮2mBZ\bm{g}=m\bm{G}_{1}^{\text{mBZ}}+n\bm{G}_{2}^{\text{mBZ}} (m,n∈ℤm,n\in\mathbb{Z}). The eigenstates of HKinH_{\text{Kin}} in valley η\eta with momentum 𝒌\bm{k} and energy ξ𝒌,mη\xi^{\eta}_{\bm{k},m} are denoted by

|ψ𝒌,m​η​σ⟩=ψ𝒌,m​η​σ†​|0⟩=∑𝒈,α,ℓμ𝒈​α​ℓ,mη​(𝒌)​c𝒌,𝒈​α​ℓ​η​σ†​|0⟩,\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{\bm{k},m\eta\sigma}}=\psi^{\dagger}_{\bm{k},m\eta\sigma}\ket{0}=\sum_{\bm{g},\alpha,\ell}\mu^{\eta}_{\bm{g}\alpha\ell,m}(\bm{k})c^{\dagger}_{\bm{k},\bm{g}\alpha\ell\eta\sigma}\ket{0}, (S83)

where mm is a band index. We work in periodic gauge μ𝒈−𝒈′​α​ℓ,nη​(𝒌+𝒈′)=μ𝒈,α,nη​(𝒌)\mu^{\eta}_{\bm{g}-\bm{g}^{\prime}\alpha\ell,n}\left(\bm{k}+\bm{g}^{\prime}\right)=\mu^{\eta}_{\bm{g},\alpha,n}(\bm{k}) such that ψ𝒌+𝒈,n​η​σ†=ψ𝒌,n​η​σ†\psi_{\bm{k}+\bm{g},n\eta\sigma}^{\dagger}=\psi_{\bm{k},n\eta\sigma}^{\dagger}. Explicitly, the μ𝒈​α​ℓ,mη​(𝒌)\mu^{\eta}_{\bm{g}\alpha\ell,m}(\bm{k}) matrix is defined by

∑𝒈,α,ℓ∑𝒈′,β,ℓ′μ𝒈​α​ℓ,mη∗(𝒌)[hKinη(𝒌)](𝒈​α​ℓ),(𝒈′​β​ℓ′)μ𝒈′​β​ℓ′,nη(𝒌)=δm​nξ𝒌,mη.\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{g},\alpha,\ell}\sum_{\bm{g}^{\prime},\beta,\ell^{\prime}}\mu^{\eta*}_{\bm{g}\alpha\ell,m}(\bm{k})\left[h_{\text{Kin}}^{\eta}(\bm{k})\right]_{(\bm{g}\alpha\ell),(\bm{g}^{\prime}\beta\ell^{\prime})}\mu^{\eta}_{\bm{g}^{\prime}\beta\ell^{\prime},n}(\bm{k})=\delta_{mn}\xi^{\eta}_{\bm{k},m}. (S84)

In this band basis, the density operator is

ρ𝒒=∑𝒌∑𝒈,α,ℓ∑η,σc𝒌+𝒒,𝒈​α​ℓ​η​σ†​c𝒌,𝒈​α​ℓ​η​σ=∑𝒌∑m,n∑η,σψ𝒌+𝒒,m​η​σ†​Λm​nη​(𝒌+𝒒,𝒌)​ψ𝒌,n​η​σ,\displaystyle\rho_{\bm{q}}=\sum_{\bm{k}}\sum_{\bm{g},\alpha,\ell}\sum_{\eta,\sigma}c_{\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{g}\alpha\ell\eta\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{\bm{k},\bm{g}\alpha\ell\eta\sigma}=\sum_{\bm{k}}\sum_{m,n}\sum_{\eta,\sigma}\psi_{\bm{k}+\bm{q},m\eta\sigma}^{\dagger}\Lambda_{mn}^{\eta}(\bm{k}+\bm{q},\bm{k})\psi_{\bm{k},n\eta\sigma}, (S85)

where we have introduced the form factors

(S87)

VI.2 Hartree-Fock calculations

For the Hartree-Fock calculations, we assume a spin- and valley-polarized state. To simplify the notation, we will suppress spin and valley indices in the following. Performing a mean-field decoupling (similarly to the parent band model) leads to the Hartree and Fock terms

HH\displaystyle H_{H} =1A​∑𝒌,𝒌′,𝒈∑m,n,o,pVcsc​(𝒈)​Λm​n​(𝒌+𝒈,𝒌)​Λo​p​(𝒌′−𝒈,𝒌′)​𝒫o​p​(𝒌′)​ψ𝒌,m†​ψ𝒌,n\displaystyle=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{g}}\sum_{m,n,o,p}V_{c}^{\text{sc}}(\bm{g})\Lambda_{mn}(\bm{k}+\bm{g},\bm{k})\Lambda_{op}\left(\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{g},\bm{k}^{\prime}\right)\mathcal{P}_{op}\left(\bm{k}^{\prime}\right)\psi_{\bm{k},m}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k},n} (S88a)
HF\displaystyle H_{F} =−1A∑𝒌,𝒌′,𝒈∑m,n,o,pVcsc(𝒌−𝒌′+𝒈)Λm​n(𝒌+𝒈,𝒌′)Λo​p(𝒌′−𝒈,𝒌)𝒫o​n(𝒌′)ψ𝒌,m†ψ𝒌,p,\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime},\bm{g}}\sum_{m,n,o,p}V_{c}^{\text{sc}}\left(\bm{k}-\bm{k}^{\prime}+\bm{g}\right)\Lambda_{mn}\left(\bm{k}+\bm{g},\bm{k}^{\prime}\right)\Lambda_{op}\left(\bm{k}^{\prime}-\bm{g},\bm{k}\right)\mathcal{P}_{on}\left(\bm{k}^{\prime}\right)\psi_{\bm{k},m}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k},p}, (S88b)

where the density matrix is 𝒫m​n​(𝒌)=⟨ψ𝒌,m†​ψ𝒌,n⟩\mathcal{P}_{mn}(\bm{k})=\langle\psi_{\bm{k},m}^{\dagger}\psi_{\bm{k},n}\rangle. We keep the nbandsn_{\text{bands}} lowest conduction bands. Some ambiguity exists in restricting HF calculations to low-energy bands [33, 13]. In our case, we implement the projection to the lowest conduction bands by restricting the band summation in Eq. (S88) to the corresponding indices. This would correspond to the “charge neutrality scheme” in Refs. [33, 22]. To solve self-consistently for 𝒫m​n​(𝒌)=⟨ψ𝒌,m†​ψ𝒌,n⟩\mathcal{P}_{mn}(\bm{k})=\expectationvalue{\psi_{\boldsymbol{k},m}^{\dagger} \psi_{\boldsymbol{k},n}}, we discretize the first Brillouin zone, introduce a momentum cutoff, and use periodic Pulay mixing in the same way as the parent band model (see Sec. II.2).

VI.3 Existence of the AHC

We briefly summarize the argument for the existence of an AHC in HF calculation of R5G that was highlighted in previous work [13, 74, 15]. HF calculations of the system at unity filling with respect to the moiré unit cell and in a strong displacement field that polarizes the conduction electrons away from the moiré potential show that interaction leads to spin and valley polarization and an isolated fully-filled Chern |𝒞|=1|\mathcal{C}|=1 band [13, 15, 74, 18, 33, 23, 22]. Since the conduction electrons are polarized away from the hBN, one may naturally wonder if the underlying moiré potential is required to stabilize the Chern insulator. To investigate this point, the ground state of the model H=HR5G+κ​HM+HCH=H_{\text{R5G}}+\kappa H_{M}+H_{C} can be tracked as the moiré potential is completely removed (κ=0\kappa=0) to see if the Chern insulator remains stable. Fig. S10(a) shows that the |𝒞|=1|\mathcal{C}|=1 Chern insulator remains lower in energy than the trivial 𝒞=0\mathcal{C}=0 insulator as one interpolates between the physical (κ=1\kappa=1) and moiréless (κ=0\kappa=0) limits. The Chern insulator also remains gapped in the continuum limit when the moiré potential is removed, as illustrated in Fig. S10(b). This indicates that HF predicts an AHC ground state that spontaneously breaks translation symmetry when κ=0\kappa=0. We note here that the HF calculations presented in Fig. S10 assume spin and valley polarization and only allow the system to spontaneously break translation symmetry with the same direction and periodicity as the moiré lattice even when it is completely removed.

VI.4 Lattice deformations

In this subsection, we describe how to parameterize distortions for R5G/hBN. One subtlety is that the lattice vectors now depend on the specific twist angle considered (see VI.1.1). The real space basis vectors (i.e., satisfying 𝑨imBZ⋅𝑮jmBZ=2​π​δi​j\bm{A}^{\text{mBZ}}_{i}\cdot\bm{G}^{\text{mBZ}}_{j}=2\pi\delta_{ij}) are

𝑨1mBZ\displaystyle\bm{A}_{1}^{\text{mBZ}} =a2​3​(ε2+θ2)​(3​ε+3​θ,3​ε−3​θ)=λM2​3​ε2+θ2​(3​ε+3​θ,3​ε−3​θ)\displaystyle=\frac{a}{2\sqrt{3}(\varepsilon^{2}+\theta^{2})}\left(\sqrt{3}\varepsilon+3\theta,3\varepsilon-\sqrt{3}\theta\right)=\frac{\lambda_{M}}{2\sqrt{3}\sqrt{\varepsilon^{2}+\theta^{2}}}\left(\sqrt{3}\varepsilon+3\theta,3\varepsilon-\sqrt{3}\theta\right) (S89a)
𝑨2mBZ\displaystyle\bm{A}_{2}^{\text{mBZ}} =aε2+θ2​(−ε,θ)=λMε2+θ2​(−ε,θ),\displaystyle=\frac{a}{\varepsilon^{2}+\theta^{2}}\left(-\varepsilon,\theta\right)=\frac{\lambda_{M}}{\sqrt{\varepsilon^{2}+\theta^{2}}}\left(-\varepsilon,\theta\right), (S89b)

where the moiré length is λM=a/θ2+ε2\lambda_{M}=a/\sqrt{\theta^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}}. The initial (undistorted) moiré lattice sites are then

𝑹\displaystyle\bm{R} =m​𝑨1mBZ+n​𝑨2mBZ,\displaystyle=m\bm{A}_{1}^{\text{mBZ}}+n\bm{A}_{2}^{\text{mBZ}}, (S90)

where m,n∈ℤm,n\in\mathbb{Z}. We distort this lattice by applying a displacement 𝒖⁡(𝒓)\bm{u}(\bm{r}), such that it can be expressed using new basis vectors 𝑨~1mBZ\tilde{\bm{A}}_{1}^{\text{mBZ}} and 𝑨~2mBZ\tilde{\bm{A}}_{2}^{\text{mBZ}} as

Let us first consider a shear deformation along the 𝑨2mBZ\bm{A}_{2}^{\text{mBZ}} direction. In this case,

VI.5 Optimal orientation of the AHC

The above HF calculations (in Sec. VI.3) assumed that the AHC crystallizes in the same direction as the original moiré lattice (i.e., the AHC lattice is described by the basis vectors 𝑨1mBZ\bm{A}^{\text{mBZ}}_{1} and 𝑨2mBZ\bm{A}^{\text{mBZ}}_{2}). However, when the moiré potential is turned off (or when it is sufficiently weak), there are no a priori reasons for this to be true. For instance, if one still assumes a triangular lattice with the same periodicity as the moiré potential, the new AHC lattice could be spanned by the basis vectors R⁡[φ]​𝑨1mBZR[\varphi]\bm{A}^{\text{mBZ}}_{1} and R⁡[φ]​𝑨2mBZR[\varphi]\bm{A}^{\text{mBZ}}_{2}, where φ\varphi is a rotation angle. It is important to note that these different crystallization orientations (i.e., different φ\varphi) are not equivalent considering the C3C_{3} symmetry of the dispersion that is induced by the trigonal warping terms in the kinetic Hamiltonian (Fig. S11(c) and (f)). For instance, Fig. S11(a) and (d) show the evolution of the triangular lattice AHC energy per conduction electron as a function of the rotation angle starting from the moiré potential aligned configuration in a strong (Ud=−36U_{d}=-36 meV) and weak (Ud=−20U_{d}=-20 meV) displacement fields, respectively. The |𝒞|=1|\mathcal{C}|=1 AHC crystallizes in the same direction in both cases as determined by the Fock term and its dominant variation (see Fig. S11(b) and (e)). It should be noted that although the rotation angle minimizing the total energy also minimizes the kinetic energy in the strong displacement field case (Fig. S11(b)), it does not in the weak field case (Fig. S11(e)). This stems from the presence of local minima in the free dispersion for Ud=−36U_{d}=-36 meV, compared to a flat free dispersion at Ud=−20U_{d}=-20 meV (see Fig. S11(c) and (d) and insets of panels (a) and (d)).

VI.6 Elastic properties of the AHC

To evaluate the AHC stiffness in R5G, we start from the triangular lattice orientation with minimal energy (Sec. VI.5). From this configuration, we apply shear and dilation deformations with strengths in the range us∈[−0.25,0.25]u_{s}\in[-0.25,0.25] and ud∈[−0.15,0.15]u_{d}\in[-0.15,0.15], respectively. We then fit the ground state energy variation to a second-order polynomial to extract the second-order derivative. The energy variation from which the stiffness reported in the main text has been deduced is shown in Fig. S12. One can observe the negative shear and dilation stiffnesses (Fig. S12(a)), indicating the presence of a mechanical instability. The variation of the different energy contributions should also be noted: the Fock and kinetic energies have a negative concavity, whereas the Hartree term has a positive concavity. This should be contrasted with the stable triangular lattice AHC found in the parent band model shown in Fig. S13. There, the kinetic and Fock terms are concave up and down, respectively (the Hartree term variation is negligible). By comparison, the triangular lattice instability of the AHC in R5G then appears to be driven by the kinetic energy. Indeed, despite a much larger Hartree energy variation that favors the stability of the triangular lattice, the triangular AHC is unstable in R5G and not in the parent band because of this opposite concavity in the kinetic energy variation.

Let us try to develop a simple conceptual understanding of these different behaviors. The upward concavity of the Hartree term in R5G is relatively simple to explain. It is well-established that a triangular network of charges minimizes the electrostatic energy in two dimensions. The Hartree energy will then increase as we distort the lattice, starting from the most stable triangular configuration.

The upward variation of the kinetic energy in the parent band as a function of distortion can also be relatively easily understood. The kinetic energy of a fermionic system with a quadratic dispersion |𝒌|2/(2​m)|\bm{k}|^{2}/(2m) is minimized by filling the lowest kinetic energy states to obtain a rotationally invariant Fermi surface in momentum space. If, instead, one fills the first Brillouin zone of a two-dimensional lattice, the lattice with the minimal kinetic energy is the triangular lattice since its D6D_{6} symmetric first Brillouin zone is the one that most closely approaches a circularly symmetric Fermi surface with the same density. The kinetic energy will then increase as the triangular lattice is deformed. Of course, this is a much-simplified argument since the diagonal part of the density matrix ultimately enters the calculation of the kinetic energy in HF. The momentum space occupation is not just a simple filling of the triangular lattice first Brillouin zone but extends much beyond that. However, this simple intuition should still apply since the momentum space occupation will remain invariant under the C6C_{6} point group operations and should thus (assuming similar spreads of the momentum space occupation at a given interaction strength for different lattices) approximate the most closely a rotationally invariant disk that minimizes the kinetic energy. For R5G in a strong displacement field, this intuition does not hold anymore since the dispersion has local minima (see Fig. S11(c)). A distorted triangular lattice that more heavily populates these local minima may then be more energetically favorable from a kinetic standpoint.

The above intuition then suggests that the triangular lattice AHC in R5G may be made stable by reducing the displacement field to remove the local minima in the free dispersion (Fig. S11(f)). We substantiate this intuition by performing a similar analysis of the triangular AHC in R5G with Ud=−20U_{d}=-20 meV. Fig. S14 shows that, indeed, the triangular lattice is now mechanically stable and that the kinetic energy has an upward concavity.
